#58. After record heat, could the Atlantic make Britain's weather even more extreme?

After record heat, could the Atlantic make Britain's weather even more extreme?

Somewhere in the stormy waters off Greenland, a bright yellow robotic probe, known as an Argo float, is sinking silently beneath the waves.

It is roughly the size of a person, with a tough metal body and an array of sensors packed inside.

The float is part of a global effort to solve one of the great mysteries of the ocean: how its hidden movements help shape the climate above.

There is no crew, no one steering it. Instead, it drifts with the currents, measuring temperature, the amount of salt in the water and pressure as it moves through the waves.

When it rises, it briefly breaks the surface and sends its data home by satellite. Then it does it all again. Dive, drift, measure, surface, transmit. The question those floats are helping investigate is one of the most important - and most contested - in climate science: whether one of the world's great systems of ocean currents is beginning to change.

It is called the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, or AMOC - a vast, north-south system of currents that carries warm surface water towards the Arctic and returns colder water thousands of miles south through the deep ocean.

The Argo float is part of a global network collecting data to help scientists understand how ocean currents shape Earth's climate

But scientists say the AMOC is under pressure. Most agree it is likely to weaken as the planet warms. The UK government has said that, as "a key component within the Earth's climate system" the AMOC contributes to the UK's long-term climate risks.

The disagreement is over how much and how fast the current could change, what that would mean for the weather and crucially, whether the seasons we know today could begin to change.

The question matters because the AMOC is part of a vast heat-moving system that influences the climate far beyond the Atlantic. But for the UK and north-west Europe, its influence is much closer to home: it helps shape the climate we live in and the weather we get.

The tropics receive far more energy from the sun than the poles. That imbalance sets both the air and the ocean in motion. Winds, storms, rainfall and currents are all, in different ways, the planet trying to even out that difference.

The UK sits in the middle of that exchange. Heat released from the Atlantic feeds into the air above it, helping fuel storms, steer winds and influence the pressure systems that reach north-west Europe. So, if the ocean changes, the weather can change too.

That includes a possibility that might seem bizarre in a warming world: changes in the Atlantic could bring more extreme swings in the UK's weather, including colder winters, even as average global temperatures continue to rise.

The AMOC includes the Gulf Stream and helps explain why Britain and north-west Europe are milder than their latitude would suggest. Its scale is hard to grasp. It carries about one petawatt of heat northwards - roughly 50 times the total energy humanity uses.

Some researchers say the warning signs are already visible: a strange patch of cooling in the North Atlantic and changes in how salty the water is.

They point to recent studies suggesting the circulation may be less stable than previously thought - raising the possibility that it could weaken sharply or even shift into a different state. In the most extreme scenario, some scientists warn it could "collapse".

Others urge caution. They say weakening is not the same as collapse, and that the evidence may point to a slower decline or reorganisation rather than a sudden shutdown.

But if the AMOC weakens significantly, it could shift storm tracks, alter rainfall and make winters more volatile.

A severe weakening, or collapse, could go further, bringing colder, drier winters to the UK and north-west Europe even as the planet as a whole continues to heat up.

Scientists say changes to the AMOC could reshape the UK's weather, bringing colder winters and changing rainfall patterns

And the consequences would not stop at the Atlantic. The AMOC helps shape rainfall and temperature patterns far beyond Europe.

A major shift could tug at the West African monsoon, tropical rainfall belts and rainfall over the Amazon. These are not abstract changes on a map: they could affect harvests, water supplies and the livelihoods of hundreds of millions of people.

Which is why scientists are watching the ocean so closely.

The floats are only part of the effort. Satellites, moored arrays of sensors and research ships are gathering data from the modern ocean too.

Other clues are much older. They lie in mud, shells, ice and rock - fragments of evidence from a time when the Atlantic appears to have changed with startling speed.

New research led by University College London (UCL), for example, looked back nearly 13,000 years to the Younger Dryas, a sudden reversal in the warming that followed the last ice age.

The cooling appears to have taken hold over just a few decades. Britain and parts of northern Europe were pushed back towards colder, more hostile conditions for more than a thousand years. In Scotland, glaciers advanced again in parts of the uplands.

For the small groups of hunter-gatherers then living in Britain, it would have been a catastrophic upheaval - forcing them to adapt or retreat as the cold returned and the landscapes they depended on changed around them.

But for scientists studying the AMOC today, the real significance of the Younger Dryas is what it reveals about the Atlantic.

The new study suggests the circulation did not just weaken. It rearranged itself. The Gulf Stream shifted hundreds of miles north, sending much warmer water towards eastern Canada.

The lead author of the study, Fangjingcheng Zhu, says the study shows the Atlantic circulation can be "abruptly altered during climate change".

For Prof Stefan Rahmstorf, that is part of a much wider warning from the past.

Rahmstorf, of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, is one of the world's leading experts on the AMOC. He has spent more than three decades studying the stability of the Atlantic circulation. From the start of his career, he says, he was interested in what ancient climate records revealed about abrupt changes in the North Atlantic currents.

The lesson, he says, was that "the paleoclimate evidence actually doesn't suggest that climate change would happen smoothly, but rather in some jumps and jolts and non-linear effects".

But for years, Rahmstorf treated an AMOC shutdown as a low-probability, high-impact risk. Serious, but unlikely.

Professor Stefan Rahmstorf says he once saw an AMOC shutdown as unlikely, but believes the risk has grown in recent years

"In the last five years or so," he says. "I really unfortunately had to change my view about the probability of this happening."

His argument begins with seawater. The AMOC depends on dense water sinking in the high North Atlantic. Cold and salt help make seawater dense.

As warm, salty surface water travels north through the Atlantic, evaporation makes it saltier. Further north, it cools. Together, those processes can make the water heavy enough to sink into the deep ocean, helping to drive the AMOC's overturning flow.

Rahmstorf's concern is not just that global warming could weaken that process. It is that, beyond a certain point, the weakening could begin to feed on itself.

Warmer surface water is lighter. Extra rainfall and meltwater from ice make the ocean fresher. Fresher water is lighter too.

If the water in the high North Atlantic becomes too light, less of it sinks. If less water sinks, the AMOC weakens. And if the AMOC weakens, it brings less salty water north.

That is the feedback loop: the current helps keep the North Atlantic salty enough for the current to keep running. Less salt makes the water lighter, so it sinks less easily and the circulation weakens further.

Rahmstorf puts it more simply: "We have this AMOC because it's salty enough in the North Atlantic. And it's salty enough because we have the AMOC. So that's a self-sustaining system."

That helps explain why one patch of ocean has attracted so much attention.

In a warming world, the ocean surface is expected to warm. But south of Greenland, part of the North Atlantic has stubbornly refused to follow the global pattern. On climate maps, it appears as a strange blue smudge in a sea of red - the so-called cold blob.

For Rahmstorf, the cold blob is one of the clearest fingerprints of AMOC weakening. If the current is carrying less warm water north, that region would be expected to warm less than the rest of the ocean - or even cool.

He says the temperature signal is only part of the story. The same region is also becoming less salty, and other studies point to changes in the Gulf Stream and signs that parts of the North Atlantic are being renewed more slowly.

"There are quite a few independent lines of evidence," he says, "that point to an AMOC slowing already well before the measurements in 2004 began."

But that is also where the caution begins. Because continuous direct measurements of the AMOC only began in 2004, the longer-term case still depends heavily on indirect evidence.

The next question is more frightening. Is the AMOC simply weakening, like a dimmer switch being turned down? Or can it flip into a different state?

Rahmstorf believes the tipping-point risk is real. He says the underlying physics was first shown in simple models decades ago and has appeared repeatedly since. "Every single climate and ocean model that has been tested for this tipping point has found it," he says.

That does not prove collapse is imminent. But for Rahmstorf, the difference between weakening and crossing a tipping point is crucial.

"Once we have crossed the tipping point," he says, "we can't do anything to stop the further shutdown."

The process would become self-amplifying, he argues. "And so basically we're losing control."

For Rahmstorf, the past shows the Atlantic can shift suddenly from one state to another, while the modern ocean is already showing warning signs of the system reinforcing its own decline.

But not all scientists read the evidence the same way.

Prof Andrew Watson, of the University of Exeter, is one of Britain's leading ocean scientists. A Royal Society Research professor, he has spent decades studying the ocean's role in climate.

Watson does not dismiss the risk. He agrees the AMOC has shifted before. "Clearly, its behaviour has changed in the past," he says. "So there's every chance that it can change again."

But he is wary of drawing too straight a line from the ice age to today - or of imagining the AMOC as a single conveyor belt that simply switches off.

The AMOC is part of the same planetary heat-moving system that drives weather itself. Heat still has to move away from the tropics. Water that rises in one part of the ocean has to be balanced by water sinking somewhere else.

One of the great engines of that wider overturning lies far from the North Atlantic, in the Southern Ocean. There, fierce winds blow almost continuously around Antarctica, drawing deeper water up from below.

Powerful winds around Antarctica help drive one of the world's biggest ocean circulation systems by drawing deep water to the surface

So if deep water formation weakens in the North Atlantic, Watson argues, the system may not simply stop. The sinking may shift. The circulation may reorganise. Warm water may still flow north, even if less of it reaches the places where it now gives up heat and sinks.

The AMOC depends on deep water forming in a handful of places in the North Atlantic - including the Labrador Sea, the Greenland Sea and waters south of Iceland. But in the ocean, Watson says, that sinking is not a simple plughole. It happens through a combination of eddies, mixing, rotation and friction close to land.

Climate models, with grid boxes often tens or hundreds of kilometres wide, cannot resolve that detail directly. They have to approximate it. "The models are good in many other ways," Watson says, "but they're not good in this particular thing."

That does not mean the AMOC is safe. It means the evidence is complex, and the future of the system cannot yet be reduced to a simple story of imminent collapse.

That caution is reflected in recent work led by the UK Met Office. In a study published last year, Dr Jonathan Baker and colleagues tested the AMOC across a range of climate models. Their conclusion was reassuring in one sense: a total collapse this century looked unlikely.

But it was not reassuring in every sense. The AMOC still weakened. And even a weaker AMOC, rather than a collapsed one, could reshape weather patterns across Europe and beyond.

Watson also points out that any AMOC weakening would unfold in a warming world. Some of the cooling influence of a weaker AMOC could be offset by the wider rise in global temperatures. Britain and north-west Europe would not be pushed back into an ice age, he says.

The effect could be more complicated: continued risk of extreme summer heat, greater exposure to cold winters, and more volatile weather generally.

Scientists say a weaker AMOC could bring more volatile weather, including extreme summer heat

Rahmstorf accepts that global warming could soften the cooling effect in average temperatures. But he argues that does not make the risk benign.

"Only the temperature impact," he says. "It enhances the drought impact for Europe, because both AMOC slowing and global warming increase drought in Europe."

And, he adds, averages can hide what matters most to people living through the changes. "This moderation may be in a climatological 30-year average temperature sense, but not for our weather."

A weaker AMOC, he argues, could sharpen the temperature contrast between northern and southern Europe - one of the gradients that helps drive storms and other extremes.

For now, the closest thing climate science has to an official judgement comes from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the UN-backed body that assesses climate research.

Its latest major assessment from 2021 concluded the AMOC is very likely to weaken this century, but that an abrupt collapse before 2100 was not expected.

But the IPCC does not update its verdict every time a new paper appears. Its assessment reflected the evidence available at the time.

Since then, the field has moved fast. New studies have sharpened concern. Others have challenged the methods behind some of the most dramatic warnings.

Watson says that uncertainty needs to be understood carefully.

"The basic science of climate change is very well established," he says. "But the AMOC is one of the few areas where models can disagree even when they start from the same assumptions. Normally, the big uncertainty is what people will do - how quickly we will cut emissions. Here, there is real uncertainty about how the ocean itself will behave."

The argument is over how close the system is to a threshold - and how much weight to give to each kind of evidence: ancient climate records, modern observations, statistical warnings and complex climate models.

The disagreement is also a glimpse of science doing its hardest work: weighing uncertain evidence when the stakes are high.

Watson's instinct is to keep the uncertainty visible. For him, caution is not complacency. It is a demand for precision.

Rahmstorf draws a different lesson from the same uncertainty. He sees a risk that is low enough to remain debated, but severe enough to demand action.

"We will not have certainty before it's too late," Rahmstorf says. "So we will have to act on our uncertainty."

The science does not offer a neat ending. It offers probabilities, warnings, caveats and arguments between experts who weigh the same clues differently.

But they agree on what is driving the risk.

The AMOC is being stressed by the warming of the planet. The more greenhouse gases humanity releases, the greater that stress becomes.

Cutting emissions does not remove every uncertainty. It does not guarantee the Atlantic will behave as scientists hope.

But it reduces the pressure on a system no society can afford to push too far.

Somewhere in the North Atlantic, the floats will keep diving, drifting and surfacing - measuring a circulation that is still moving, still mysterious, and still capable of surprise.

Whether the AMOC is simply weakening, or being pushed towards something more abrupt, remains unresolved.

But the safest response is already clear.

#59. Why cheap power could matter more than clean power in the push for net zero

Why cheap power could matter more than clean power in the push for net zero

"I'm an early adopter of new technology," says Gavin Tait, a 69-year-old from Glasgow, with a hint of pride.

So when he received a lump sum on retirement a decade or so ago, he invested in renewable energy: solar panels on the roof, a home battery and a heat pump. "It seemed like a no-brainer," he recalls. "I could save money and help the environment - why wouldn't I?"

At first, it worked. His well-insulated home stayed warm and his energy bills fell. But when electricity prices surged after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, costs rose, and over the past couple of winters, things began to change. "I noticed my electricity bills were going through the roof," he says.

This winter, he and his wife switched it off and went back to their gas boiler, which they had kept as a backup.

Gavin - who wrote in to BBC Your Voice about his experiences - says he knows what the problem was. At best gas delivers nearly one unit of heat for each unit of energy put in; his heat pump can deliver up to three or four units of heat for every unit of power. But as heat pumps run on electricity, he is now paying around 27p per kilowatt-hour, compared with less than 6p for gas that powers a boiler - more than four times as much.

While he is on a smart tariff with a cheaper overnight rate, it lasts just five hours, so he's paying the higher rate most of the day.

One of the issues affecting Gavin's bills is scale. Gavin bought his battery roughly 10 years ago and it is only 1.5 kWh - the best he could afford at the time, but too small to store enough electricity to make much difference.

Gavin Tait and his wife switched off their heat pump and returned to their gas boiler after rising electricity costs made it too expensive to run

And there's another issue. Gavin says he's happy to have the house at 19C or 20C but his wife sometimes turns up the thermostat to 23C. Heat pumps have to work significantly harder than gas boilers to reach higher temperatures, which can increase their energy use - and cost.

"It's simple," he says. "Economically, it just doesn't stack up."

His experience is not unusual. A survey of 1,000 heat pump owners last summer, carried out by Censuswide for Ecotricity, found two-thirds said their homes were more expensive to heat than before.

For critics of government policy, stories like Gavin's point to a deeper problem.

Heating and transport account for over 40% of the UK's emissions but they say that progress on replacing gas boilers and petrol cars is lagging well behind targets because ministers have got the wrong focus.

In their view, the government is obsessed with cleaning up electricity generation, even though it accounts for a far smaller total of our emissions - around 10%. So that obsession is pushing up the price of electricity and making it more expensive for people to switch to a heat pump or electric vehicle.

The issue has taken on new urgency as conflict in the Middle East pushes up oil and gas prices, raising fears that high energy costs could persist.

Conflict in the Middle East, particularly tensions around the Strait of Hormuz, has pushed up oil and gas prices

The government insists that focusing on renewables will ultimately deliver greater energy security by reducing reliance on imported gas, lowering emissions and - crucially - cutting bills.

Are they right? Or by prioritising cleaner electricity while progress on heating and transport lags behind, is the government chasing the wrong targets?

The issue is that while generating renewable electricity can be cheap, the system needed to deliver it is not. When I ask Sir Dieter Helm, professor of economic policy at Oxford University, for his definitive answer on the cost of renewables, he laughs.

"It all depends what you choose to measure," he says. Sir Dieter says focusing only on the cost of generating electricity misses a larger issue: the cost of the system as a whole.

Electricity has to be available all the time - not just when the wind is blowing or the sun is shining. That means back-up generation, additional capacity and a more extensive network.

Energy secretary Ed Miliband is leading the government's green energy push

Sir Dieter gives me a simplified example. The UK's peak electricity demand is around 45 gigawatts (GW), he says. In the past, this could be met with roughly 60GW of capacity from coal, gas and nuclear power stations.

As the system shifts towards renewables, far more capacity is needed - not just wind and solar, but back-up for when they are not producing. In Sir Dieter's estimate, the UK is moving towards something closer to 120GW. At the same time, the grid must also be expanded to carry electricity from offshore wind farms to where it is needed.

The exact figures are debated, but the direction is clear: partly because of renewables, the system is becoming larger, more complex and more expensive. Some of those costs are already showing up in bills. Expanding the grid - building new pylons and power lines - is pushing up network charges.

There are also "balancing costs", including payments to wind farms to switch off when the system cannot absorb all the electricity they produce. And until recently, a subsidy scheme accounted for around 10% of the average household bill.

There is another issue. The UK is richest in one of the more expensive renewable resources - offshore wind.

Solar power has seen dramatic cost reductions thanks to mass production. But Britain's often dull skies - especially in winter, when demand is highest - limit how far it can carry the system.

Offshore wind is more dependable but it involves large, site-specific engineering projects that cannot be replicated in the same way, and so have not seen the same sustained falls in cost. At the same time, rising prices for materials such as steel and rare earths - along with higher interest rates - have pushed costs up further.

On paper, the UK has made significant progress on going green — the nation's emissions are down by around 50% since 1990. But that does not necessarily mean the UK's overall global footprint has fallen by that much.

Many of the goods that were once produced and then used in Britain are now being made overseas and then imported here, and often that production is happening in countries with a higher carbon footprint.

China, for example, still relies on coal for more than half of its energy, meaning emissions simply have shifted abroad rather than been reduced altogether.

This is a point made by leading climate scientists including Prof Kevin Anderson of Manchester University, who argues the 50% figure "excludes international aviation and shipping and our imports and exports".

He adds: "If you include those, which of course the climate includes, then the reduction's about 20% since 1990." The government says it follows United Nations guidelines on emissions reporting.

China still relies on coal for more than half of its energy, raising concerns that emissions linked to UK consumption may simply have shifted overseas

At the same time, the higher system costs do not just show up in household bills - they ripple through the wider economy. UK households face some of the highest electricity bills in Europe. For businesses, the picture is even starker.

While the cost of renewables plays a part, the principal driver for this is, ironically, gas itself. The UK energy mix at any one moment usually includes plenty of renewables, but some gas is still frequently still needed. The way the market works, generators bid to supply power in half-hour blocks, with the cheapest bid accepted first. But all successful bidders end up being paid the price of the most expensive source needed to meet demand.

In practice, that source is usually gas. So, even when much of the electricity is generated from renewables, which are cheap to produce once you get past the hefty set-up costs, it is often gas-fired power stations that set the price - and therefore what everyone pays.

The system is widely used across Europe, but the UK's heavy reliance on gas has a clear consequence: when gas prices rise dramatically as in recent weeks, electricity bills tend to rise with them - even if much of the power itself is renewables that are cheap to produce.

The UK's comparatively higher energy costs have coincided with a wave of closures among energy-intensive industries. Sharon Todd, chief executive of the Society of Chemical Industry, described the impact of energy costs as a "national act of self-harm", warning that UK industry is "standing on the edge of a cliff" and calling for an urgent independent review of the country's approach to net zero.

It is against this backdrop that the politics of climate change has begun to shift.

When then Prime Minister Theresa May set the 2050 net zero target in 2019, it passed without formal opposition in Parliament. That consensus has since fractured.

The Conservative Party now argues the target is "impossible", with leader Kemi Badenoch openly sceptical. Reform UK says it would abandon what it calls "net stupid zero" altogether. Even the Green Party has criticised aspects of government policy, with its leader, Zack Polanski, saying the current approach to net zero is not delivering for ordinary people.

The Liberal Democrats also say net zero must support households and bring down energy bills. The SNP says it is "absolutely committed to a fair and just transition to net zero", while Plaid Cymru recently moved away from its earlier ambition of reaching net zero in Wales by 2035.

Under Kemi Badenoch's leadership, the Conservatives argue the UK's 2050 net-zero target is "impossible"

Polling suggests the public appears to still support the decarbonisation effort. More in Common found that four in five Britons think it is important that the government cares about tackling climate change, including nearly 80% of 2024 Conservative voters.

What really concerns people is cost. Data from the Office for National Statistics shows the cost of living is cited by around nine in 10 adults as an important issue, with energy bills among the most frequently mentioned pressures on household finances.

This is where the argument about focusing on lower energy prices and decarbonisation comes in. The economists and politicians who make this case say that it would both help keep the public onside on decarbonisation and drive more rapid emissions reductions.

Their argument is simple: if electricity is cheaper, more people and businesses will switch to technologies like electric cars and heat pumps - and emissions will fall faster.

The highest-profile intervention to date has come from former UK Prime Minister Sir Tony Blair. His Tony Blair Institute for Global Change last year called for a shift in focus from the government's "Clean Power 2030" agenda to "Cheap Power 2030".

The Tony Blair Institute for Global Change has called for a shift from the government's "Clean Power 2030" agenda

The "clean power" logic is that a cleaner grid will make everything that runs on electricity, from cars to heating, cleaner by default. Supporters of a "cheap power" approach argue that is only part of the story. The bigger prize lies in cutting emissions from the sectors that use energy, not just how that energy is generated.

Reducing emissions therefore depends on persuading people to switch to electric technologies such as heat pumps and electric vehicles. But, as the experience of Gavin Tait - the Glasgow homeowner - shows, that decision often comes down to cost.

If electricity is expensive, households and businesses have little incentive to make the switch. If it is cheaper, the transition becomes easier - and faster.

Tone Langengen, senior policy adviser on climate and energy at the Tony Blair Institute and the author of its recent report, argues that the focus should shift away from targets and towards what will bring down the cost of energy.

In her view, every decision on energy policy should be judged through the prism of whether it reduces prices.

"The sooner we move from a debate focused on targets to one focused on how you structurally change the economy and decarbonise in a way that works both economically and politically," she says, "the faster we will move on climate action."

Heat pumps work for me - but they're not yet a money saver

How the rise of green tech is feeding another environmental crisis

Britain's energy bills problem - and why firms are paid huge sums to stop producing power

But turning that idea into policy is not straightforward. Every option involves trade-offs - between prices, emissions and public spending.

Sir Dieter, the Conservatives and the Tony Blair Institute all argue that slowing the pace of renewable expansion, and maintaining a larger role for gas in the short term, should be part of the answer. But while using fewer renewables could ease pressure on system costs, it risks slowing the pace of emissions cuts.

Energy Secretary Ed Miliband says renewables bring other benefits too. "The lesson of yet another global energy shock is that the UK needs to get off the fossil fuel rollercoaster and onto clean homegrown power that we control," he says.

"Driving for clean energy is a national security and economic security imperative- that is why this Government is investing record amounts in new renewables, nuclear, and upgrading homes through our Warm Homes Plan."

Other proposals raise similar tensions. Reforming the way the electricity market works could reduce the amount providers get and therefore reduce bills. Shifting some policy costs from electricity bills to general taxation could lower prices but would place greater strain on public finances.

When I press Langengen on how electricity prices could be reduced in practice, she acknowledges there is "no magic wand". She argues that "speaks to the credibility of the argument". But it also highlights just how difficult those choices are.

For some economists, that difficulty points to an even more uncomfortable conclusion - one that goes to the heart of political leadership.

Sir Dieter says we need to face up to a hard truth: tackling climate change costs money.

Sir Dieter says tackling climate change comes with a hard truth that it will cost money

Fossil fuels are cheap in part because their price does not reflect the damage they cause - from rising temperatures to impacts on health, property and the natural world. Cutting emissions means bringing those hidden costs into the price of energy. And that has consequences.

"My costs go up, my bills go up and my standard of living goes down," says Sir Dieter. There is, he argues, no easy way around that. "The evidence suggests it is going to be more expensive."

That presents a dilemma for governments. The bet behind today's push for clean power is that countries, like the UK, can show it is possible to decarbonise the grid without imposing unacceptable costs - and in doing so, lead the way for others.

The Office of Budget Responsibility has said "the costs of failing to get climate change under control would be much larger than those of bringing emissions down to zero." But achieving that requires global emissions cuts.

There is also the argument that getting oﬀ gas quicker reduces vulnerability to price shocks. But there is a risk. If the transition here in the UK drives up costs and erodes public support, it will not be a model to follow, but a warning to avoid.

And yet the urgency of cutting emissions is not in doubt. The World Meteorological Organization warns the Earth is now further out of balance than at any time in recorded history, with the planet absorbing far more heat than it can release. As the UN Secretary General António Guterres has put it, "every key climate indicator is flashing red".

If Sir Dieter is right, governments will have to be honest: the transition will cost more. The challenge - and it is a tough one - is persuading the public it is worth it.

Clarification 18 May 2026: The article has been updated to include further information about the running costs of Gavin Tait's heat pump.

#60. Microsoft pulls out of UK's largest AI data centre

Nscale said it remained committed to building a £2bn AI data centre in Loughton

A tech company has said it still plans to build the UK's largest AI data centre despite Microsoft pulling out of the project.

Nscale announced last year it had pledged £2bn to build and open a pioneering facility in Loughton, Essex.

However, the BBC understands that Microsoft, which said it would fund a supercomputer at the site, has terminated its involvement.

A spokesperson for Nscale said it was exploring alternative power sources and its relationship with Microsoft remained strong for their other projects together overseas. Microsoft declined to comment.

"We remain committed to both the Loughton project and the UK and we are exploring alternative power sources for the site, in addition to other expansion sites in the UK," Nscale said.

"Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term."

What is the new AI supercomputer planned for Essex?

The data centre was due to receive its power supply at the end of the year.

But as first reported by the Telegraph on Sunday, external, Nscale has been told this will not happen until the 2030s.

"This unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts," Nscale told the BBC.

Nscale and Microsoft are still working together on projects in Norway, Portugal and the United States.

The Loughton site is expected to create 250 permanent jobs when it eventually opens.

Only last month, Microsoft announced that some of the $30bn (£22bn) it was investing in the UK would be used to fund the Loughton supercomputer.

#61. Home sellers cut asking prices on 3,000 properties a day

Home sellers cut asking prices on more than 3,000 properties a day on average in Britain during September, according to figures from Rightmove shared exclusively with the BBC.

The property website said the total was the highest of any month for 15 years and was driven, in part, by a glut of homes on the market and some sellers setting unrealistic expectations.

The proportion of listed homes that eventually had a price cut peaked in 2023 and has remained relatively high since.

Property portals say buyers are now having to be choosy, with many working to a tight budget as mortgage rates have risen to three-year highs.

"Once a home has been on the market for a while and then has a price reduction, some buyers start asking questions, even when there is nothing wrong with the property," said Colleen Babcock of Rightmove.

"In a market with so much choice, first impressions matter."

Rightmove data said the average price reduction was nearly 7% - the equivalent of nearly £21,000 cut from a typically valued home.

Its data showed that homes that had a price reduction typically took 119 days to find a buyer, compared with 39 days for those listed at one price.

The proportion of listed homes that had a price reduction stood at 34% in last month, only slightly lower than the recent peak of 36% seen in September 2023.

Rival property portal Zoopla said that buyers were in the driving seat, and were being more cautious and selective about the properties they viewed.

With mortgage rates at a three-year high, Zoopla said buyers needed to keep monthly mortgage payments affordable.

So, while the number of homes for sale was up 5% in September compared with a year earlier, the number of sales agreed had fallen by 9% over the same period, its figures showed.

September also tends to be the month with the most cuts to asking prices as sellers often want to complete a sale by the end of the year.

Zoopla's data showed that a quarter of newly-listed homes in September had previously been listed for sale in the last year. Six in 10 were returning at a lower asking price.

The problem for sellers was that these homes were taking longer to sell.

Properties that needed a price reduction were half as likely to find a buyer within the normal three-month timeframe, according to Richard Donnell, executive director of research at Rightmove.

'Our flat has been for sale for four years': Why is the market so weak?

You need £17,000 for a first home - here's how to save it

Sellers who have contacted the BBC's Your Voice have pointed to the difficulties created by lots of homes on the market, and extra problems for those selling leasehold properties in England.

One, who was selling his late father's home in south Wales, said: "The market is dead. Lots for sale; no-one buying. No-one thinks it's going to get easier."

Tarah Lourens, chief operating officer at Rightmove, said that "emotional" factors influenced sellers pricing a home - as they "put a value on the time and money they have invested in their home".

But she said that buyers simply considered everything they could buy at their budget.

Agents said that valuations now drew on huge amounts of data. Craig Webster, of Tiger Sales and Lettings in Blackpool, said that getting an initial price correct when new to the market was crucial.

"That's when you have the greatest opportunity to capture the attention of active buyers," he said.

Katie Griffin, from surveyors Sawdye and Harris in Devon, said that having to correct a price could ultimately lead to a seller accepting less than even a revised asking price.

"The property may already have been online for several months and buyers can start asking why it has not sold," she said.

But Andrew Boast, chief executive of SAM Conveyancing, said sellers might still not be losing out, if they had negotiated aggressively when buying the home and had seen it rise in value while they owned it.

In Scotland, the Home Report system, external requires an independent valuation of a home before it is put on the market.

Donnell, from Zoopla, said the system gave sellers a guide to pricing. As a result homes sold at a faster rate than anywhere else in Britain.

His data showed that 74% of homes in Scotland listed during April, May and June sold within three months, compared with 30% in London.

He said that higher prices, stamp duty and some people - including landlords - not needing to sell meant that listed homes were less likely to sell in southern England.

#62. People playing loud music on buses could face £100 fine

Passengers who play loud music on buses in England could be fined up to £100 under an attempt by the government to crack down on antisocial behaviour.

The measures also seek to tackle littering, vaping and threatening behaviour to help improve journeys on all forms of public transport.

Offenders on buses could be issued with the fines under new powers for local authorities.

A national campaign asking rail passengers "share the carriage, not the noise" is also being launched. The proposed crackdown has been welcomed by campaigners, but some have questioned how it can be enforced.

"We've all been on the train when someone starts blasting music or videos from their phone. It gets on your nerves and can quickly spoil the journey," said Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

Under existing powers, those who are asked to stop and refuse could be removed from a train or fined up to £1,000.

The phenomenon has been given many terms - including loudcasting or sodcasting - and in recent years, Ofcom, YouGov and Transport for London (TfL) have all published polls showing the vast majority of people dislike it.

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said small changes in behaviour "can make a massive difference to people's experience on public transport".

The government said it had issued new guidance to local authorities on powers - which were introduced earlier this year - to help them crackdown on loud music and other antisocial behaviour on buses in England.

These new powers allow them to impose new rules on buses, but still need to be signed off by the Transport Secretary

Those who commit offences could face fixed penalties of up to £100.

The government says bus drivers will not be responsible for enforcing the new rules. It says authorised officers, including Transport Safety Officers and the Police, will deal with the incidents.

Meanwhile a new national campaign aims to remind rail passengers to "share the carriage, not the noise", to improve journeys for everyone

The campaign will be launched across operator websites, social media, and in carriages. The government said this would end the current "patchwork" of approaches across different rail operators, and help create "a clear, consistent message across the network".

The general secretary of the TSSA transport union, Maryam Eslamdoust, said tackling antisocial behaviour on public transport was "a step in the right direction".

However, she added that the government must also "urgently confront the violence, threats and abuse faced by passengers and transport workers".

"Increasing the budget for British Transport Police is vital to protect people, respond to incidents and bring violent offenders to justice," she said.

Michael Solomon Williams from the Campaign for Better Transport told the BBC antisocial behaviour could be a "real deterrent" to people using public transport, especially those with different accessibility needs.

He also questioned how the new measures will be enforced. "When local authorities are required to do the enforcement there are perhaps some question marks about how a local police force might be called upon on bus services, for example, where we don't tend to see British Transport Police."

Richard Holden MP, Shadow Transport Secretary, said: "After we led the charge against antisocial behaviour on public transport last summer, Ministers have worked out that nobody wants to endure pounding techno or blaring hip hop on a packed train or bus.

"But passengers and railway staff face far more serious problems. Assaults against rail staff have risen by 68%, while prosecutions have slumped under Labour. It's time for Andy Burnham to get serious about enforcement, tackling violence and protecting those who work on our railways."

Liberal Democrat Transport spokesperson, Olly Glover MP said: "Tough talk means nothing without enforcement.

"Unless the Government funds transport safety officers on the ground, these new rules won't be worth the paper they're printed on."

Independent watchdog Transport Focus said research it had published in June showed personal safety and security was now fundamental to passengers' confidence in the railway.

"Four in 10 passengers say that anti-social behaviour has made them feel vulnerable when travelling," said Alex Campbell, Transport Focus's director of policy and insight.

"Measures that reduce nuisance behaviour, such as playing loud music and vaping, can help improve people's experience and encourage more people to choose public transport."

#63. EU tariffs aimed at China hitting Ukraine, steel boss says

The boss of one of Ukraine's biggest steel companies has called on the European Union to drop import restrictions on products made from the country, arguing it has been "bundled together" in measures aimed a curbing cheap imports from the likes of China.

Yuriy Ryzhenkov, chief executive of Metinvest, told the BBC the recently-imposed tariffs on imported steel to the EU were "unfair" and had been put in place "without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in".

He said he wished to see "at least a carve out" for Ukraine to access the EU market.

A spokesperson for the European Commission said the EU "took into account the difficult situation" of Ukraine when deciding its steel policy.

The trading bloc has recently imposed restrictions on steel imports in an effort to protect steel manufacturers of member nations.

It has capped the amount of steel which can enter the EU tax free at 18.3 million tonnes per year - a 47% reduction from 2024 levels.

There are some country-specific quotas in the policy, but the overall aim is to cut the amount of steel that can be imported due to member nations struggling to compete with cheap imports from the likes of China and Turkey.

Despite a free-trade agreement (FTA) being in place between the EU and Ukraine, the FTA does not stop the EU from introducing separate trade protection measures.

"Ukraine has been bundled together into those measures without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in," Ryzhenkov said, pointing to the war with Russia.

"Access to the European market is crucial for survival," he added. "The restrictive measures that have been put in place by the authorities in the European Union, they don't help.

"I think it's unfair that Ukraine has been treated in the same way as all of the other importers into the European Union."

The Ukraine steel industry estimates steel exports to the EU could ultimately fall by about 50–60%.

The EU said Ukraine's specific steel quota guaranteed exports of the metal, but acknowledged this was at a "level lower than in the past years".

"Despite the war effort, Ukraine remains an important exporter of steel to the EU," a spokesperson said, adding it had "offered compensations" to its largest suppliers, which included Ukraine.

Yuriy Ryzhenkov, chief executive of Metinvest, says EU steel quotas are "unfair" on Ukraine

Steel products are a foundation in Ukraine's economy. Before the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, metallurgy and mining accounted for roughly 10% of Ukraine's national income and a third of its exports. The EU is its top customer.

But the industry has suffered from the continued Russian bombardment.

All of Ukraine's steel mills have been bombed at points since the conflict began in 2022, but Ryzhenkov said strikes had "intensified significantly recently".

At one point in September, there was "no single tonne of steel produced" in Ukraine for the first time in about 150 years, he added.

Almost 800 Metinvest workers have been killed since the war began.

Ryzhenkov said the company had "improved the covered areas" at its mills where workers can shelter during air raids.

"The only thing we can do is to design procedures to keep people safe and just obey those procedures and try to minimise the risks."

"Unfortunately, you cannot cover a whole steel mill to avoid it being damaged."

Ryzhenkov said he expected the coming winter to be "one of the hardest in our history".

"We are in a dire situation when we don't have logistics to access any other market apart from the EU and cutting our available market by 60%, that doesn't help for the industry to survive."

#64. There's a crackdown on sports piracy - but is it already out of control?

There's a crackdown on sports piracy - but is it already out of control?

"Football's Gone Round the Spend!" screamed The People newspaper one Sunday in July 1995. It reported breathlessly that three clubs between them were set to pay out more than £20m on new players.

The highlight that summer was the transfer of Stan Collymore from Nottingham Forest to Liverpool for a British record fee of £8.5m.

That number might not seem too impressive today, in an age when £100m transfers are almost commonplace. But at the time it was seismic stuff, and it symbolised the conversion of football from sport into big business.

All of this had been made possible in the early 1990s by the creation of the Premier League, and its initial TV deal with the broadcaster Sky, which paid more than £300m for five years of rights. The agreement put live top-tier football behind a TV paywall for the first time.

It was a lucrative model, one that other leading championships in motorsport, rugby, golf and cricket would later seek to replicate.

But now, that model is coming under pressure. Piracy has become endemic in British sports: around half of sports fans now admit to using what they might euphemistically call "alternative" means to watch paywalled material, according to the consultancy Ampere Analysis.

This year's Champions League final - won by Paris Saint-Germain - sparked an argument about TV viewing rights

And this summer saw signs of a clampdown.

In August, a man in Lancashire was jailed for six and a half years for running an illegal streaming service that police said had generated almost £1m in illicit profits. In June, a postman from Pembrokeshire was jailed for over three years for selling illegal subscriptions and supplying pirate software to nearly 2,000 people.

A third man, from Merseyside, received a suspended 32-month sentence in August for similar offences. Several pubs have been fined thousands of pounds for screening matches illegally.

TV companies that have paid huge sums for exclusive rights to high-profile sports are having to work harder than ever to protect their investments. To some extent, broadcasters used to see copyright theft as a cost of doing business: irritating and expensive, but not an existential threat. But now, as advertising revenues fall, and viewers move away from long-term subscription services like Sky or TNT Sports, the industry is getting seriously worried.

There is a great deal at stake. The Premier League alone is a sporting monster. In its most recent deal, it sold its viewing rights to domestic audiences for £6.7bn over four years, with almost as much coming from foreign rights. Armed with bundles of TV cash, clubs have been able to attract the finest players in the world. That in turn has given the league a major international profile.

Although football has been the main beneficiary of paid-for TV in the UK, other competitions such as Formula One, Six Nations rugby and the Wimbledon tennis championships have also commanded very high fees for selling exclusive rights. Live sport on free-to-air television has become increasingly rare.

Yet that wealth could be threatened by a surge in piracy and illegal viewing. The practice is most common among younger, digital-native audiences, who each year become a larger and larger share of sports fans. But many older viewers also seem comfortable with it.

Rupert Murdoch (left) launched Sky TV with the broadcaster Andrew Neil in 1989. It went on to transform Britain's sports-watching landscape

"For 18 to 34-year-olds, it's over 70% who admit to doing this regularly," says Daniel Monaghan, a researcher at Ampere Analysis. "Over half of 35 to 44s admit to doing it, and about a third of those aged 45 to 64."

This year's Champions League final went behind a paywall in the UK for the first time in more than 30 years. Viewers were asked to pay at least £4.99 to watch it, prompting a backlash, including from the then-prime minister, Arsenal fan Sir Keir Starmer.

"Hardworking people shouldn't have to fork out for a subscription to watch this match," he wrote on X.

Many simply refused to pay: 3.7 million IP addresses accessed illegal streams of the match in the UK, according to research carried out by the Gaming Compliance International consultancy, on behalf of the Guardian newspaper. That compared to around seven million people who watched it legally in the UK.

One prolific user of pirate streams is "Kiran", a tech sector worker in his 30s, who prefers not to give his real name. A keen Arsenal fan, he likes to watch Premier League and Champions League games, as well as big matches in Spain's La Liga. He has a paid subscription to TNT Sports, but uses streaming websites to see games that are not available there.

Many fans watched this year's Champions League final legally at pubs - but at home, 3.7 million IP addresses accessed illegal streams of the match, according to one analysis

"What it comes down to is the financial side - that's the big one - and ease of access as well," he says. "Getting every single game will cost you hundreds of pounds a year."

Meanwhile the streams he uses are free, with links readily obtainable on social media.

But there's another issue, he says: the famous blackout. Games taking place between 14:45 and 17:15 on a Saturday are not usually screened live in the UK, a decades-old policy designed to protect crowds at lower league matches. But broadcasters outside the UK can and do show those matches, fuelling pirated streams.

"I pretty much got into streaming stuff due to [the blackout]," Kiran says, "and I'd say I sort of did it a bit more as subscriptions got more expensive."

Those searching for pirated material have plenty of options. Streaming links, along with advice on how to avoid their pitfalls, are freely available in online discussion groups. These links, used by Kiran and his friends, have practical downsides – such as frequent buffering or poor quality, or platforms that disappear without warning. In some cases, they can also be used to bombard viewers with explicit ads for porn sites.

Many people prefer to access illegal content with a streaming device, such as an Amazon Fire Stick, a pocket-sized gadget that plugs into a TV. The sticks are legitimate products, but they can also be "sideloaded" with unauthorised software, allowing pirates to mimic the output of legitimate outlets by offering packages of selected channels.

A third option for illicit viewing is to use a virtual private network, or VPN, which effectively allows your computer to pretend it's in a different country, one in which access to sports programming is cheaper than it is in the UK (or totally free).

Earlier this year, the Sports Industry Group found that 58% of fans surveyed considered illegal streaming to be socially acceptable.

Stan Collymore's transfer from Nottingham Forest to Liverpool, for £8.5m, set a British record in 1995

That may be because viewers have simply come to resent the amount of money they are expected to pay.

As the government's Intellectual Property Office puts it, "a main driver of illegal content access is the perception of unfair or high pricing for legal services".

A British person wanting to access all live Premier League games, for example, would need subscriptions to both Sky Sports and TNT Sports. Throw in some matches from Spain, or European Champions Cup rugby, and Premier Sports has to be added to the list. Many boxing matches and NFL games are on DAZN. A keen fan could easily end up paying £80 to £100 a month.

Until relatively recently, clamping down on piracy was not seen as a priority by the broadcasters themselves. They were focused on audience growth, and copyright infringement was simply a cost of doing business.

Formula 1 is another sport that's been able to command high fees for selling exclusive TV viewing rights

In some parts of the industry, it was even seen as a benefit. In 2013, the then-chief executive of Time Warner, Jeff Bewkes, notoriously welcomed the drama series Game of Thrones becoming the most pirated show in the world. He suggested that the attention generated by illegal viewing was "better than an Emmy" because it helped create buzz and ultimately attract new subscribers.

Now, however, the mood has shifted. Conventional broadcasting is under pressure as advertising revenues fall and viewers move away from long-term subscription services, towards more flexible offers from streaming platforms such as Netflix, Amazon Prime and Apple TV. Both Sky and TNT Sports have reported losses.

According to a recent report by WPI Economics, illegal sports streaming costs the broadcasting industry about £700m each year.

And piracy is already having impacts on the pitch.

At a conference last year, Tom Burrows, the head of global rights at the sports streaming platform DAZN, described piracy as a "huge problem" for his company, and "almost a crisis for the sports rights industry".

Just months after he made those comments, DAZN agreed to end its deal with the French football league, under which it was allowed to screen the top tier of French football matches within France. The agreement followed a bitter dispute, which focused in part on the streamer's claims the league had not done enough to combat piracy – although subscriber numbers were also understood to be an issue.

Even though DAZN paid a reported €100m (£85m) to end the contract (along with outstanding rights fees worth another €140m), its departure created a hole in the French league's finances. It was left to set up its own streaming service, and the amount of broadcast income fell from roughly €700m per year to €412m this season, according to figures compiled by football-finance.com.

For a European powerhouse like Paris St Germain, with plenty of other revenue sources, this probably matters little. But for smaller teams it has been a serious problem. Angers SCO, a club in the west of France, said last year the affair had cost it €30m over two seasons, and forced it to sell its striker Estéban Lepaul.

It's unlikely that a competition on the scale of the Premier League would lose its broadcaster. But piracy could ultimately limit how much they will be willing to pay in future.

The French club Angers SCO was forced to sell its striker Estéban Lepaul last year

"If you look at the finances of some of the broadcasters, they're losing money," says Kieran Maguire, associate professor of football finance at the University of Liverpool. "Piracy… is taking up a larger and larger share of the revenues that they would anticipate being able to generate through their subscription models. So yes, it is a worry for them."

Daniel Monaghan of Ampere thinks piracy "is at the very least a significant constraint on the sports rights models that have been highly lucrative for broadcasters and rights holders over the last 30 years".

If left unchecked, he thinks this will make it harder for rights holders to generate a return on their investments.

At best this could hamper future growth. At worst it could lead to falling revenues over time, hitting the sports that have benefitted most from the wave of TV money.

In the case of the Premier League, this might just mean fewer blockbuster transfers - but it could also reduce the sum the League gives to the wider football game, from grassroots upwards, which amounted to £1.6bn over the three years to 2025.

A key part of the solution, according to the industry-funded Federation Against Copyright Theft (Fact), is changing attitudes among consumers.

Nick Sumner, the organisation's investigations manager, insists piracy is not a victimless crime. "Organised crime is behind this, and they want to make money by any means possible," he explains.

It also leaves users at risk of fraud, he warns. "They capture… a lot of personal data, which they can then sell for criminal gain."

Broadcasters and sporting bodies have been working hard to shut off illegal online streams. Hundreds of thousands are taken down each year. But tackling them is, as Monaghan puts it, like whack-a-mole: "Some get taken down, others come up, often in different countries."

In the UK, downloading or streaming pirated content can be a crime. Yet the chances of viewers themselves being prosecuted for watching a cheeky Saturday game on a pirate stream are extremely low.

The £5 coffee that tells a story of global economic turmoil

Europe's car makers are in crisis. Will the threat of war rescue them?

Why some experts increasingly fear AI will take over

Nick Sumner of Fact says the current priority is to educate people about the risks of piracy - but he conspicuously stops short of ruling out a more punitive future policy.

"There are crimes being committed here," he says.

So it is possible that viewers of illicit material just might one day find themselves in expensive legal trouble.

However, the sheer scale of a major clampdown would present a formidable challenge, and could generate resentment. There would be no guarantees that those watching illegally today would take out legitimate subscriptions tomorrow.

#65. Third runway at Heathrow Airport would drive growth, Healey says

British Airways planes lined up at Terminal 5 at Heathrow Airport

Chancellor John Healey has said building a third runway at Heathrow Airport has "always been a case for growth" after Prime Minister Andy Burnham refused to say if he backed the expansion.

Healey said airport expansion, including at Heathrow, had been "a big part of jobs and growth" in recent decades, speaking at the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in Bangkok.

His comments came after Prime Minister Andy Burnham was more sceptical, telling the BBC last month it was "a matter for London and Londoners".

Healey's predecessor Rachel Reeves had put the airport's expansion at the centrepiece of an argument that Britain was open for business.

Earlier this week Heathrow's chief executive Thomas Woldbye warned that not building a third runway at the UK's busiest airport would be a "huge missed opportunity".

Healey told reporters: "The case for a third runway at Heathrow has always been a case for growth."

He added: "The formal position now is that the consultation is closed, led by the Transport Department.

"We're reviewing those, and then further decisions and announcements will follow."

The third runway been debated for decades, with the project facing opposition from residents, politicians and climate campaigners.

Last year, Reeves announced the government-backed expansion, saying "a third runway is badly needed", and the government could not "duck the decision any longer".

Asked about the project in September, Burnham suggested it was an argument for London to decide.

"I think we ought to hear the voice of people there first. It's not right for me to just jump straight in on the back of the consultation," he added.

The Department for Transport has said it is "considering the appropriate next steps" following the public consultation on its National Policy Statement, which provides the basis for deciding whether to grant a new runway at Heathrow.

The airport's consortium of owners has said they need explicit backing from Burnham before the end of the year in order to proceed with the project.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme earlier this week, Woldbye said it would be "good to know" the government's position on the project.

He said he hoped the prime minister would "come along" with the project, adding that a third runway was "not just for Londoners".

"Benefits will be felt all over the country because our supply chain reaches all the way from the north all the way to the south of the UK," Woldbye said.

Heathrow serves more than 80 million travellers a year with its four passenger terminals and two runways. The number of flights, currently capped at 480,000 a year, could go up to 720,000 - or nearly 2,000 a day on average, if a third runway is built.

The project, which has an estimated price tag of £33bn, would see hundreds of homes demolished, rivers diverted and the M25 motorway rerouted through a tunnel between junctions 14 and 15.

The new runway was scheduled to open by 2035, subject to plans being submitted and approved, but Heathrow has since suggested it would be delayed by four years to 2039 due to planning and regulatory issues.

#66. Faisal Islam: Why China and AI are worrying global finance bosses

When it comes to the future direction of the global economy there is a bit of a tug of war going on.

There are starkly opposing forces. On the one hand holding back growth are the familiar, recurring crises from the energy shock, trade conflict and actual war. This is reflected most clearly in the sharply rising interest rate costs for the world's advanced economies.

Pulling in the other direction is the boost from massive spending on AI, and the frankly astonishing resilience shown especially by smaller economies, as new routes for trade, including for oil and gas, have been established out of necessity.

At the IMF meetings in Bangkok this week these themes came up again and again, including among those at the very top table. But not even they know which way things are going to go.

In the meantime it's a sportsman's bet where the roving eye of the bond markets will focus next. Currently they seem to be looking at the US and France.

However, the French finance minister, Roland Lescure, has been telling the world he has had no problem selling debt, though it was more expensive, and that his Budget would be fine. He also suggested he had helped save the G7 group of advanced nations, which was at risk of collapsing a year ago amid Donald Trump-inspired tensions.

In some ways it is a miracle there has not been a global recession, or a debt crisis in a major emerging economy. Indeed the Thai finance minister was boasting to me of how little his borrowing costs had gone up, especially in relation to the US.

Another surprise is the UK being taken off the bond markets' naughty step, and instead being named model pupil by the IMF. The IMF has taken the government's Budget plans at face value and on trust. The reality is that the rest of the G7 lack even this. And beauty is relative, especially when it comes to borrowing.

And this moment gave Chancellor John Healey the chance of a hearing, to highlight that the UK's actual growth data has continued to outperform expectations and so far in 2026 can now be described as strong. Healey told me that he saw the figures as the first sign that AI and tech investment was starting to increase UK economic growth. The bond financiers milling around the IMF meetings seem to be taking another look at the UK after years of crisis.

Faisal Islam: What surprise praise for UK economy tells us about the Budget

'Come all the way' back to EU, French finance minister tells UK

Three things we've learnt about the UK economy from the IMF

But there is a third big challenge to wrestle with, on top of geopolitical instability and bond market uncertainty, one that's apparent even on the streets of Bangkok, as the chauffeurs dropped off the bankers and finance ministers for this week's gathering.

Like other nations Thailand has experienced first hand the astonishing boom in sales of Chinese electric vehicles. Thailand is sometimes dubbed the "Detroit of Asia" for its own strong car making heritage. Now nearly a third of all car sales are Chinese EVs.

It is the clearest example of what is known as the China Shock Two. The sheer speed of China's dominance in advanced manufacturing. The first China shock came in the 2000s in basic manufacturing.

This second wave of dramatic change has led in just the last few months to a reappraisal of how world trade is functioning and how it is going to be managed. This is especially the case in the EU, which is scrambling to reassess what currently feels like a one-way street when it comes to China-Europe trade.

The extra "Made in Europe" protections that the bloc is drawing up will have a profound impact on the UK too. If the UK is outside the new rules, China could divert its excess car production to the UK, where, like Thailand, there are currently lower tariffs and even subsidies. Or the EU could invite Britain in, but ask it to follow its suit by raising tariffs to match its own.

Then there is the sub-plot of the UK's relationship with the European Union. This was a theme that cut through more than might have been expected in Bangkok this week and even seemed to provide a little entertainment. The managing director of the IMF Kristalina Georgieva rolled with laughter, suggesting the Brexit "divorcees are now dating again". The Finnish finance minister told me the UK was "flirting" with the EU. Major banks were issuing reports about the prospect of "Breturn".

It is, however, the AI boom that is being relied on to provide the trampoline that is required to bounce the world economy out of its current era of multiple simultaneous crises, so many of which are linked to the decisions of President Trump.

But even that is not clear cut. In one room the transformative economic effect of AI is lionised by finance ministers. In the next, central bankers fret about its power to break the cybersecurity of most of the banking system. The financial boom around it can't last. The masters of the financial universe are just thankful that it has so far.

#67. What is the Budget and what could be in it?

Chancellor John Healey will set out Labour's tax and spending plans when he delivers his first Budget on 28 October.

He has refused to rule out tax increases after acknowledging government borrowing costs are at "historic highs".

But the government's room for manoeuvre on tax is limited.

Before the 2024 general election, Labour promised not to increase three big revenue earners for the government: income tax, National Insurance and VAT.

In his statement, delivered to MPs in the House of Commons, Healey will set out how the government plans to raise or lower taxes.

Alongside the Budget, the Treasury will publish details about the measures and their costs.

The independent Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), which monitors government spending, will also publish an assessment of the health of the UK economy and a forecast of what it thinks will happen in the future.

The run-up to the Budget typically generates speculation about what might be in it, which the government is trying to keep to a minimum this year.

Healey and Prime Minister Andy Burnham face a difficult balancing act, trying to offer more support to households and meet commitments on defence spending, while also sticking to Labour's manifesto commitments on tax and the government's self-imposed fiscal rules.

The previous chancellor, Rachel Reeves, set out two main rules, which the new leadership has vowed to follow. These are:

Not to borrow to fund day-to-day public spending by the end of this parliament

To get government debt falling as a share of national income by the end of this parliament

In March, the OBR calculated that the first rule would be met with a gap - or headroom - of £23.6bn. However, this headroom is expected to have shrunk.

Analysts are divided on how much it may have fallen by. KPMG believe it could have fallen to £12bn, mainly due to the rise in government borrowing costs this year.

The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) also forecasts that debt interest will significantly reduce headroom. But it also suggests higher inflation could push up tax revenues as pay rises drag people into higher tax thresholds.

It estimates the buffer could still shrink but to a comparatively less severe £20bn.

One option that has been floated is that Healey could decide to accept a smaller buffer, reducing the need to increase taxes in the Budget.

Bank bosses have told the BBC they expect Healey to raise taxes on the sector. UK banks have been reporting bumper profits, leading to calls from unions for higher taxes.

The Treasury has options: it could raise a 3% surcharge on profits which was lowered from 8% under the previous Conservative government, or it could raise the bank levy that is based on the size of their balance sheets.

Further details on the "Your First Home" scheme, aimed at helping first-time buyers in England to purchase a property, are expected to be announced in the Budget.

The scheme will allow people to buy a new-build home with a deposit of 2.5%. It would provide them with a loan worth 20% of their property's value to help pay for the purchase.

There has been speculation that Capital Gains Tax (CGT) - which is imposed on the profit people make when they sell an asset that has increased in value - could be changed, through either higher rates or by removing or amending exemptions.

At the moment, if you pay income tax at the basic rate then CGT is charged at 18%. For higher and additional rate income tax payers, the CGT rate is 24%.

The FT has reported, external that Healey has rejected proposals to raise CGT to the same rates as income tax.

The Times has reported, external that online retail giants such as Amazon and eBay are expected to be made responsible for collecting tax owed by traders using their platforms.

The paper said the money raised is expected to be used by the government to cut business rates for High Street shops, by raising the threshold at which small companies start paying rates from £12,000 to £18,000.

Fuel duty was frozen under the Conservatives in March 2022 and Sir Keir Starmer's government continued the freeze, deciding in May to push back a planned 3p increase in September until the end of this year.

Healey told the BBC in late September that the "place" and "time" for dealing with rising petrol and diesel costs was the Budget, but would not give details on whether the freeze would be extended again.

Household energy bills are set to see their biggest rise in four years in January, with a typical annual bill forecast to jump by £276.

There has been speculation, external that Healey is planning energy bill help for households on certain benefits.

The High Value Council Tax Surcharge - dubbed the Mansion Tax - was announced in last year's Budget and will apply to properties in England valued above £2m from April 2028.

There had been speculation that the government was considering extending it to properties worth more than £1.5m. However, reports now suggest, external Healey has ruled this out.

In the first three months of the year, the UK's economy grew by 0.6%, while in the April-to-June quarter it grew by 0.5%.

The most recent data showed the economy grew by 0.1% in August after growth of 0.4% in July, with both figures being stronger than expected.

Analysts say the UK economy is proving resilient in the face of energy price shocks caused by the US-Israel war with Iran.

The conflict has led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for oil and gas trade. This caused a sharp jump in oil prices, which has fed through to higher energy and fuel prices.

Economists expect UK growth to slow in the months ahead as those costs continue to weigh on households and businesses.

Prices for goods and services are still rising faster than wanted. Inflation hit 3.1% in the year to August, the highest rate in five months and above the Bank of England's 2% target, driven by higher petrol and diesel prices.

The Bank of England held interest rates at 3.75% for the sixth time in a row in September, but said they were likely to rise if high energy prices persist.

The Budget speech usually starts at about 12:30 UK time - after Prime Minister's Questions - and lasts about an hour.

It will be broadcast live on the BBC iPlayer and on the BBC News website.

The Leader of the Opposition, Conservative MP Kemi Badenoch, will respond to the speech in the House of Commons.

MPs debate the measures for four days, before voting on them.

If approved by MPs, tax changes can come into effect immediately.

However, the government must pass a finance bill to make them permanent.

#68. 'I took a chance on the whisky industry and I haven't looked back'

Zoey Darnbrough took a job at Annandale Distillery after finishing her studies

Zoey Darnbrough is the first to admit that just a few years ago she did not even know there was a whisky distillery near her hometown in southern Scotland.

But it hasn't stopped her rising rapidly from tour guide, to group tourism and events co-ordinator at the site near Annan.

She went away to study heritage and tourism in Stirling after school, but unlike many of her peers, she returned to Dumfries and Galloway for work.

Now she hopes to play her part in changing people's opinions of the world of whisky "one woman at a time".

Annandale distillery shut in 1919 before reopening 90 years later

The 26-year-old, who attended St Joseph's College in Dumfries, was recently nominated for "rising star" recognition at the South of Scotland Thistle Awards.

Zoey said her journey had not been straightforward as she did not get the exam results she had hoped for at school, so she spent time working in the kitchens at Dumfries Infirmary.

But when a job came up at Annandale Distillery, she jumped at the chance.

She said: "My first thought was - there's a distillery in Annan? And my second thought was - whisky?

"I thought I'd give it a chance and see what it was like because there's a lot of heritage when it comes to whisky.

"And I've now been here three-and-a-half years and I've not looked back."

Revived distillery toasts first 10-year-old malt

What does she think the area has to offer that others her age might ignore?

One thing she highlighted was the relative costs of property compared with city prices.

Zoey also believes the area has a lot to shout about and is happy to have returned after university.

"The south of Scotland has so much heritage and it is a passion of mine," she said.

"So I would naturally like to be somewhere where there's a lot of heritage and where I can kind of grow as an individual."

Zoey is passionate about what the south of Scotland has to offer

But she agrees that a lot more could be done to stop young people from leaving.

"I would like to think we could go back to the local schools across the region and try and explain that there are other careers out there including in heritage and tourism," she said.

Zoey would also like to see the area market itself better.

"We've got so much to offer in terms of castles, in terms of scenery, in terms of attractions, accommodation, it's so vast," she said.

"I always like to say that we've got everything that the Highlands have, but just in a much quieter area.

"But we're going to use that quietness to our strength."

What stories would you like BBC News to cover from the south of Scotland?

She has certainly achieved that in her own career in the whisky industry - despite some people assuming she might lack the knowledge of older, male counterparts.

"It has been tricky, I'm not going to lie," she said. "But I always think that if you prepare yourself well, those types of questions cannot faze you.

"I've been so fortunate that all my experiences have been mostly pleasant and so I have not really felt it, but I do understand the struggles that other people face.

"We just need to start changing people's opinions one woman at a time."

Zoey is happy to do that from Dumfries and Galloway for the foreseeable future.

"I'm only beginning to stick my teeth into the south of Scotland," she said. "So to leave, it would have to be a fairly big jump."
