#109. Marvel fans to meet Welsh superhero - complete with Cardiff accent

Cardiff-born actor Lauren Morais is "very proud" to bring her accent to the MCU

Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from the VisionQuest series

Marvel fans around the world are set to meet a Welsh villain - complete with a Cardiff accent.

Lauren Morais, from the Welsh capital, will play Lisa Molinari in the new superhero series VisionQuest - a spin-off from the miniseries WandaVision.

The Disney+ show, exploring whether AI and humanity can co-exist, also stars Paul Bettany, returning as Vision, and James Spader as Ultron.

Morais, 25, said getting the role was a "pinch me" moment and that she was "very proud" to introduce her accent to the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU).

Speaking to Lucy Owen on BBC Radio Wales, Morais said she initially auditioned with an Essex accent for the part.

In the fourth round of auditions, she also did a northern accent and American.

But during a reading, not knowing if the Marvel team wanted a Welsh accent, Morais decided just to "go for it".

"I said, 'can she be from Cardiff?' and they were like, 'of course'. So she's from Cardiff now," she said.

The cast of VisionQuest at the series' UK premiere in October

Morais will follow in the footsteps of Catherine Zeta-Jones who used her Swansea accent in Kill Jackie, a Prime series which follows a former cocaine dealer who is being targeted by hitmen.

The actress said it was important to hear different accents on screen.

"There's a myriad of accents in the UK and sometimes people forget there's so many sick accents around... I think it's so nice that we've got that representation," Morais added.

She said it was a "pinch me" moment when her agent called and told her she got the part.

"I just exploded! I said 'are you sure? Are you joking?' Then an hour later I had to go to a cast dinner," she said.

I got to use my Welsh accent as a lead in the new Marvel series

Lauren Morais from Cardiff talks about her role in the new Marvel series, VisionQuest. She speaks to Lucy Owen about the evolution of how her villain character became Welsh.

Morais recalled being like "a rabbit in the headlights" surrounded by all the stars of the show, but was also worrying about who was going to cover her shift at a cinema in London.

During the audition process she was given time off for the VisionQuest auditions, even though she could not tell her manager what the auditions were for.

She said: "I went to my final Pinewood audition and then went back to the cinema to the west end to finish my shift.

"It's such a dichotomy of worlds and that's what it is as an actor, you're always grafting and then it happens and you're like, what is life."

The character of Lisa Molinari has undergone a transformation from the original Marvel comic book character - known as Coat of Arms - who gains extra arms and weapons from a mystical coat.

In VisionQuest, she is instead given a high-tech backpack equipped with robotic arms.

Morais said co-ordinating the choreography for the fight scenes was "funny".

"I'd be with the fight director who was like 'you just need to imagine that a huge arm is coming out of your right side and just absolutely go for it and imagine where it's hitting.' So I used a lot of imagination on that job," she said.

But Bettany, whose character Vision is an android attempting to piece together his wiped memories and fragile humanity, had some sage advice.

"He said 'you're going to feel very silly while you're doing these scenes, but if you commit to it, it's going to look really sick'. And I can confirm, he was right," she said.

Lauren Morais will play Lisa Molinari in the new superhero series VisionQuest

The MCU has seen a Welsh character before - the role of Welshpool appeared in Deadpool and Wolverine in 2024.

Wrexham AFC striker Paul Mullin played the surprise role as a Welsh version of Ryan Reynolds' character Deadpool.

It is not the first time Marvel fans will have heard a Cardiff accent, as Kingsley Ben-Adir, who played Gravik in Secret Invasion, previously told Buzzfeed he looked to Butetown, in Cardiff, when developing the character.

Morais said she was very proud her character had a Cardiff accent.

"I'm just so proud to be from Wales, I love it, that's why I wanted my accent in it," she said.

"I love Welsh people, I love Wales, let's go for it."

#110. Sally Rooney books withdrawn in UK over Palestine Action support

Sally Rooney has sold more than six million copies of her novels globally

Normal People author Sally Rooney has said her novels will no longer be supplied to booksellers in the UK as a result of her support for Palestine Action.

The Irish novelist said last year she intended to carry on using her royalties to support the group, which is a proscribed terrorist organisation in the UK.

In a statement to BBC News, Rooney said further publication of her work could constitute a "serious criminal offence", so she had agreed with her publisher Faber not to continue supplying her books to UK retailers.

"I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions, and I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences," she said.

Ebook editions have already been removed from sale in the UK, although many book shops still have existing stock of physical copies.

Waterstones confirmed to the BBC that Faber had advised there were no restrictions on booksellers keeping their current copies on the shelves.

Rooney has sold more than six million books globally, including 2.3 million in the UK, according to NielsenIQ BookData.

Normal People was published in 2018 and turned into a hit TV series two years later, effectively launching the acting careers of Paul Mescal and Daisy Edgar-Jones.

Rooney's other novels are Intermezzo, Conversations With Friends and Beautiful World, Where Are You.

Publisher Faber told BBC News: "Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work.

"To sell a writer's work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher.

"As such, and in full agreement with Sally, we have taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format."

Faber added: "We remain the proud publisher of her remarkable body of work, which we will continue to sell in other territories."

Rooney's four novels, including her most recent, Intermezzo, will be removed from sale in the UK

The UK government proscribed Palestine Action as a terrorist organisation in 2025, saying it had a "long history" of criminal damage.

The group's activities have included targeting arms companies linked to Israel's war in Gaza.

In her statement on Wednesday, Rooney said: "In July 2025, the direct-action protest group Palestine Action was proscribed as a terrorist organisation in the UK.

"The following month, I wrote an opinion piece expressing my intention to go on supporting Palestine Action, which is not a proscribed or otherwise prohibited group here in the Republic of Ireland."

In her article last August in the Irish Times, Rooney said she would continue using proceeds from her work to support the group despite that being an offence in the UK, and cancelled a UK trip to pick up an award over fears she would be arrested.

In her statement on Wednesday, Rooney continued: "As a result, the fulfilment of contracts to publish my work in the UK could now constitute a serious criminal offence.

"After a process of consultation and deliberation, and with my full agreement, my publisher Faber has therefore determined that it can no longer supply my work within the UK."

Palestine Action co-founder Huda Ammori said Rooney had taken "a brave and principled stand from the moment plans to ban Palestine Action were announced".

Ammori said the author's work being withdrawn marked "a new low in the escalating assault on free speech caused by the proscription of Palestine Action".

More than 3,700 people are believed to have been arrested in the UK over alleged support of Palestine Action.

About 2,500 have been charged, although none have gone to trial as a legal challenge to the proscription continues and will be heard by the Supreme Court next month.

#111. 'People call them pervert glasses': Blind users fear backlash over smart tech

Fraser Fleming says his glasses help him navigate public transport and read street signs

Fraser Fleming approaches the corner of a busy Glasgow city centre street and asks his smart glasses to describe the road ahead.

A voice coming from tiny speakers in the arms of the specs tells him there are several parked cars and a person walking in his direction.

For 44-year-old Fraser, who is registered blind, this is "game changing" information.

"I know how to approach the street and what sort of care to take," he says.

"If I need to maybe take my time or if I can just walk at normal pace."

Fraser, who began losing his sight in his early twenties, says his AI-powered Meta smart glasses have become part of his everyday life during the past two years.

They help him to navigate public transport, read street signs and order from menus – but he's started to think twice about wearing them in public.

"People are calling them pervert glasses," he says, referring to multiple reports of them being used to secretly film and harass people, particularly women and girls, with the footage being shared online.

Fraser says this is having a negative effect on anyone wearing them, including visually-impaired people.

"We are definitely not using them to record people in dodgy situations," he says.

"We're using them to lead an independent life."

They were labelled 'pervert glasses'. Will a camera-free version transform their image?

The Meta glasses revolution - is it okay to film people in public?

TikToker faces police probe over secret filming using 'smart glasses'

Fraser, from Motherwell, told the BBC's Your Voice he would often take his glasses off if he thought there was a chance of a confrontation.

"I've got enough to worry about getting from A to B," he says.

"I'll just put the glasses away and have to rely on my other senses in order to navigate around, which is going to make life a lot more difficult for me."

Tracey Rogerson says the technology is a big part of her independence

Tracey Rogerson, who uses the technology to help with her sight loss, shares Fraser's concerns.

"I was shocked to hear that they were being called pervert glasses because for me, they're such a big part of my life to help me maintain my independence," she says.

Meta, the company that owns WhatsApp, Facebook and Instagram, started selling smart glasses in 2021, and has sold about two million pairs since February last year.

It says there is a light on the frames which makes it clear the smart glasses are recording, but it also warns users not to engage in harmful activities.

As a result of the backlash against the glasses, some venues and events have banned or at least restricted their use over fears about covert filming, including ComicCon Scotland, which takes place in Edinburgh later this month.

This means Gordon Brown, who is severely sight-impaired and has attended the event with his family for the past three years, won't be going this year.

He says the impact of the ban on people with disabilities has been overlooked.

"Even if I was to put my glasses on quickly, just to read a sign or something, I wouldn't feel comfortable," says Gordon, from Inverkip.

"I think it's a matter of principle now, the fact that they're not willing to engage, and they're not willing to listen to a minority group.

"You know, we're not talking about thousands of people all of a sudden turning up wearing smart glasses."

Monopoly Events, which runs some of the biggest comic and entertainment conventions in the UK, announced in July that it had banned Meta glasses to "stop secret filming" of guests and attendees.

The ban applies to Meta glasses and other "wearable recording devices."

The company was contacted by the BBC about Gordon's comments.

Cosplay artist Spill The Tea says she was secretly filmed by someone wearing the glasses

Cosplay artist Spill The Tea was at a comic convention in Birmingham earlier this year when she was secretly filmed.

She later discovered the footage was posted online.

The performer, who has 1.9 million followers on TikTok, says she felt "violated".

"He was purposefully trying to provoke me or purposefully trying to make strange comments to get a reaction out of me so that he could get that perfect clip that he could post on social media and capitalise off it," says the London-based artist.

She says her experience demonstrates why restrictions are needed, but she thinks there should be exceptions for people with disabilities.

"For people who need the glasses and who really have to use them, I think they should be able to use them," she says.

"They shouldn't have to deal with the fact there's been a certain group of people who have spoiled it for them."

In a statement, Meta said: "We are proud that our AI glasses give blind, low-vision and hearing-impaired people greater independence in daily life.

"They were built to be noticed, which is why every pair with a camera has a bright light on the front that blinks when you take a photo or video.

"It cannot be turned off and the camera is disabled if someone covers or tampers with it."

#112. Not sure what to wear for Halloween? These outfits are set to be the most popular this year

If you're still on the hunt for the perfect Halloween costume, then you might want to look to gargoyles, Freaky Nikki and Dolly Parton for inspiration - they are all predicted to be popular outfit choices for 2026.

"People don't necessarily want to look frightening - they want to look extraordinary," says costume designer Tamar Zaig, who runs a fancy dress hire shop in London and says she's seeing a "real appetite for escapism, glamour and a bit of dark humour" right now.

And as usual, the year's major film and TV releases, as well as news and pop culture trends, are also driving outfit choices.

By order of the Traitors, channel your inner Claudia

The Traitors is a timely choice, with host Claudia Winkleman's look easy to pull together. Think fringe, tartan, chunky knitwear and some heavy eyeliner.

Winkleman is "a classic that we see every year", says the creator behind the popular Love of Huns Instagram account (who did not want to be named). But she "will definitely be making a return this Halloween off the back of all the Traitors love and the icon that she is".

Released at the beginning of the summer, ice hockey romance drama Off Campus sees characters Allie and Dean attend a Halloween party dressed as J-Lo and Top Gun's Maverick

Ice hockey romance series Off Campus also features in many of the outfit inspiration videos trending online.

The show's main characters, Dean and Allie attend a Halloween party in the series, with Allie dressed as J-Lo and Dean as Top Gun's Maverick, which could provide a rather meta costume opportunity for fans or couples.

Another of this year's most popular TV shows, Widow's Bay - which scooped up at this year's Emmy Awards - is also inspiring outfits.

Maria Nichol, 35, a horror aficionado from Ely in Cambridgeshire, plans to dress as Kate O'Flynn's character Patricia - and is trying to replicate her gothic headdress, which includes antlers and a taxidermy fox, by crafting her own from foam clay, foil and fur.

Inde Navarrette's character, Nikki, in Obsession is providing huge costume inspiration

One of the most replicated outfits looks set to be Nikki from indie horror film phenomenon Obsession, say fancy dress shops, influencers and make-up artists.

The character's red and black zebra print top went viral earlier this year, selling out online and reportedly leading to a 27,000-person waitlist, external before returning to stores.

"We've had customers asking for Nikki," says Muhammad Rai from shop Fancy Dress Town in London, with people trying to recreate her with a red corset and wig, "although unfortunately, we currently have none in stock".

"I've had a few people ask me to do that make-up for them," adds special effects make-up artist and prosthetics designer Meg, from Liverpool.

Meg (left), from Liverpool, took inspiration from Buffy the Vampire Slayer during a previous spooky season

We might also see a surge in 1990s and 2000s nostalgia, believes Nichol, with party-goers dressed as Buffy, Hilary Duff and characters from Practical Magic, after the film's sequel was released last month.

Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman cast a spell in Practical Magic 2

Gothic horror: Jessie Buckley in The Bride! and Margot Robbie in Wuthering Heights

As well as Obsession, some of this year's other top grossing films – such as the Michael Jackson biopic, Spider-Man: Brand New Day and The Odyssey – are also on the cards.

Look to ancient Greek epic The Odyssey for costume opportunities

"I'm seeing a lot of Gothic romance and historical influences not only in films such as Wuthering Heights, The Odyssey and The Bride!, but in fashion too, with corsets, lace, dramatic silhouettes appearing on the catwalks, particularly at London Fashion Week," says designer Zaig.

"Along with Peaky Blinders, I think these kind of productions have brought some great theatrical costume styles back into the spotlight, from elaborate period gowns and Greek mythology to 1930s glamour."

Ready to scream? Horror franchises Scream 7 and Scary Movie 6 will likely provide inspiration

Classic horror franchises such as Scream and Scary Movie (Scream 7 and Scary Movie 6 were both released this year), should also not be overlooked, say fancy dress shops.

Ghost face masks from Scream have made up 20% of sales at Hollywood Fancy Dress in Bournemouth, says the shop's head manager Ben Cook.

Meanwhile, characters from hit series Wednesday and Bridgerton are likely to make a return. And outfits from KPop Demon Hunters – which won best animated film at this year's Oscars - are the current biggest seller for children, according to Cook.

Demand for Dolly Parton-style stage outfits are in demand from those wanting to pay tribute to the music icon

It's not just fictional characters who might be joining your Halloween night out.

"I also expect to see plenty of instantly recognisable personalities, from the iconic Dolly Parton with her extravagant wigs and rhinestones to political figures such as Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin," says Zaig.

Rai from Fancy Dress Town also says blonde wigs, cowboy-style waistcoats and microphones are in high demand, following the death of Parton aged 80 in August.

Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin could prove to be popular outfit choices

Meanwhile, pop icons Charli XCX and Madonna could make a good duo costume, suggests Love of Huns, following the pair's collaboration on remix Danceteria Afterhours.

"Both have had enough iconic looks between them, so there's plenty to work with."

Other fresh pop culture references could include Mariah Carey and The Last Supper, after the star became a meme for sharing a selfie with the Leonardo da Vinci painting in Milan,, external they add. It's "a strong option" that "requires very little arts and crafts ability" – "a blonde wig and an A3 piece of card with The Last Supper printed on it and you're pretty much there".

"Low effort, high impact, and the sort of costume that makes absolutely no sense to anyone who hasn't been keeping up with online pop culture."

Pop icons Charli XCX and Madonna could make a good duo costume

Or another option that could make people smile is the ready-to-drink cocktail brand Buzzballz, Love of Huns suggests. "We know it's been done before, but dressing up as your favourite flavour is a fab opportunity to show off a bit of creativity."

The whimsical fashion trend, which has dominated social media feeds in 2026, is also predicted to be a big influence this Halloween for women. Think gargoyles, moths, mushrooms, woodland fairies and 17th Century Pierrot clowns.

In keeping with the theme, Lauren Sidebottom, a TikTok beauty and fashion creator from Leeds, is planning on dressing up as a weeping angel.

The 23-year-old, who studied theatrical makeup at college, says she'll be creating the look using body paint, grey tights, a cracking makeup effect on her skin, drawn-on tears, and a grey wig.

Women her age are, she says "wanting to look cool, different, not like every other girl," with their whimsical costumes.

Tiggy Bellinger, 21, from West Sussex, agrees DIY costumes can help avoid people wearing "the exact same thing".

Tiggy says while many trending costumes are easy to buy online, she wants to encourage people to look in their wardrobes and explore charity shops

She has also been sharing whimsical Halloween looks online, including a mime artist, the Very Hungry Caterpillar and a ladybird.

She uses clothes she already has or can borrow, and a bit of creative DIY, to create her looks, with the aim of encouraging others to do the same instead of buying ready-made outfits from fast fashion retailers.

"The fun thing about making costumes and Halloween is the creativity and finding bits and pieces that match and, you know, making things," she says.

Sophia dressed as Lady Liberty last year, and previously dressed up as Violet Beauregarde from the film Charlie and the Chocolate Factory - which she says cost just the price of the wig

This is also the case for Sophia, 25, who lives in Cambridge and is using a long blonde wig and pink dress she already owns to dress up as Hannah Montana, to chime with this year's anniversary special.

"Even if you just notice that you have one colour, like, 'Wow I have a lot of purple' or 'I have a lot of this sparkly material that I don't get to wear often', and thinking about what characters or what object even that that could remind you of, I think you could get something really creative that other people wouldn't have."

#113. Street Fighter movie is 'made by fans for fans' - but can it KO the critics?

Noah Centineo and Andrew Koji play Ken Masters and Ryu in Street Fighter

Video game fans have been treated to a two-hit combo of big screen adaptations recently.

First came Resident Evil, director Zach Cregger's movie version of the long-running horror game series.

The next contender is Street Fighter, the arcade classic fighting game that's been separating fans from their loose change since 1987.

Both have been turned into disappointing live-action films before.

But Cregger's attempt at Resident Evil, which impressed both critics and fans, seemed to break the curse.

BBC Newsbeat spoke to Street Fighter cast members Noah Centineo, Callina Liang and Andrew Koji to find out why they think the action movie can do the same.

The film, directed by Kitao Sakurai, follows Ken Masters, played by Centineo, and Ryu, played by Koji.

The two characters - long-standing icons of the games - are martial artists who trained under the same teacher before their relationship went sour.

Chun-Li, played by Liang, recruits the pair to compete with other elite fighters in the World Warrior tournament, organised by crime boss M. Bison.

The large ensemble cast includes about 15 characters from different instalments of the video game series, and is packed with references and Easter eggs.

"It's absurd, it's wild, it doesn't take itself too seriously," Centineo tells Newsbeat.

"And everyone who made it loves the world of Street Fighter. Grew up playing the game, loves the game."

He says it was "extremely important" for the film to stay faithful to the series, describing it as "a movie made by fans for fans", who can expect "meticulous" attention to detail.

The film recreates details including Street Fighter's famous car-smashing minigame

Centineo says the film's stunt team closely studied each character's video game movements to ensure their signature moves were accurately depicted on film.

His co-star Liang says her intense training regime was designed to help her replicate character Chun-Li's famous moves and distinctive, muscular look.

"I was eating 12 eggs a day, like, 4,000 calories, training a lot," she says.

"My motto the whole time was just 'give it your best and some more'".

Liang says she wanted to put work in "for the fans" but does stress she was careful not to take things too far.

Her fellow actor Koji thinks it's a winning formula.

"I think we've got the right approach, got the right cast, right energy," he says.

"I think we could feel it when we first read the script."

Callina Liang's performance as Chun-Li has been well-received

The Guardian called it a "garish and incoherent mess",, external but praised Liang as "formidable" and complimented her "genuinely impressive" fight scenes.

Gaming website IGN described the film as getting off to a "stylish start",, external but said it "increasingly feels disconnected from any sense of reality, even its own" along the way.

There was almost universal criticism of the "confusing" and "chaotic" plot, but some reviewers did praise the fight choreography and visuals of the film.

It's a contrast to Resident Evil, released last month, which was almost universally praised by critics and hit $300m at the global box office four weeks after release.

But will fans show up for Street Fighter?

Tayyib Mahmood, who uploads film and video game reviews to his tsreeltalk accounts, says he enjoyed Street Fighter.

"I think that it was true to what the games are," he says.

"It's taking these characters and putting them into these costumes which are unrealistic, it embraces how ridiculous these games are.

"You've got the different fighting styles, you've got these larger-than-life characters and I think the movie commits to all of that and I think there is a lot of personality to this film."

Film reviewer and Street Fighter fan Tayyib Mahmood says he enjoyed the film

Mahmood says he has criticisms of the film, such as a weak story, but thinks the attention to the "visual identity" of Street Fighter is impressive.

He also points out that fandoms of specific video games don't always agree on what would make a good adaptation.

"I don't think that every movie needs to be loved universally," he says.

"I think that sometimes a film knows exactly who it's for and I think it does need to commit to audiences and accept that other people might hate it."

#114. At the Brooklyn shop in 'surreal' row with Kelly Clarkson over mechanical bird

Watch: What's going on between Kelly Clarkson and a Brooklyn store bird?

On a rainy Wednesday afternoon, a novelty toy and games store in a quiet part of New York City was seeing much busier foot traffic than usual.

Inside, the shop was packed with cameramen and customers, while passersby in this Brooklyn neighbourhood of Cobble Hill looked inside, asking: "Where's the bird?"

Art of Play has found itself at the centre of a social media storm since the weekend when Grammy-winning musician Kelly Clarkson complained online that the boutique store would not let her buy a singing and dancing mechanical bird that was perched on the wall.

The Since U Been Gone singer claimed she was "looked at as if I couldn't afford" the bird - which she said had a price tag of $15,000 (£11,000).

"Y'all should go check out Art of Play in Brooklyn if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts' character in Pretty Woman," she said, referring to a scene from the 1990 romantic comedy film where Roberts' character is treated poorly by staff at a shop, who imply she cannot afford various items.

In a follow-up post on social media, Clarkson said the store had told her the bird cost $15,000 and that they could find her something else "comparable".

Art of Play has defended how it treated the star on social media, saying the wooden bird - which is called Molly - is permanently attached to the wall and is not for sale.

It said that during Clarkson's five-minute visit on Saturday, an employee suggested to her that she could buy an identical bird for $15,000.

They also said they had offered her a different singing bird for $2,000 from a clock-making shop in Germany, which she could have purchased that day.

"Imagine our surprise when our small local business was suddenly attacked by eight million people who have never visited our store," Art of Play said.

"It's been a surreal experience to be the focus of such widespread outrage after just one mention by a celebrity."

Molly the mechanical bird now has a price tag of $15m

Clarkson defended her decision to criticise the store on social media, saying: "I never blast people but you my friend were an exception."

When the BBC visited the store on Wednesday, there were more reporters than customers.

A shopkeeper said they would not comment on the story anymore and just wanted to get back to business as usual.

Molly still hung on the wall at the shop, this time next to a price tag of $15m.

The sign jokes that the sculpture is the "world's most famous singing bird automata!"

The store's owner has said he and his staff have faced threats and harassment after Clarkson's complaint, telling the BBC's US partner CBS News that the singer had endangered them.

This week, a man filmed himself yelling expletives outside the store, before accusing its employees of "racially profiling" Clarkson.

Customer Emily Trantanella likes Art of Play

The kerfuffle lingered in headlines on Wednesday as a news outlet released surveillance video from Art of Play purporting to show Clarkson's visit.

The grainy footage, which has no audio, is said to show her wearing a yellow shirt, a baseball cap and a backpack while browsing items, including Molly the bird.

She can be seen talking with an employee - apparently about the bird as she points at it - and later moving to leave the store. She comes back in to say something animatedly to the cashier.

But while the argument over the bird has gone viral online, some of Art of Play's customers had not heard about it before being greeted by news cameras on the premises.

One customer who was in town visiting his daughter said he was not familiar with the controversy.

For others, Clarkson's claims that those at the store had treated her rudely came as a surprise.

Kiran Ramineni, who lives next door, described Art of Play as a "very nice small mom and pop store" and said he had seen flocks of journalists there in recent days.

Shopgoer Emily Trantanella, 27, said: "I feel like a pretty woman and I've always been treated very well here.

#115. How Breaking Bad's RJ Mitte changed the way we see cerebral palsy

'Disabled or not, everyone deserves an opportunity,' RJ Mitte says in 2015 BBC interview

"I have cerebral palsy but I've never let it hold me back."

Those are the words of a 22-year-old Breaking Bad star RJ Mitte in an essay for Huffpost, external back in 2014.

Explaining his experiences of learning to stand up to bullies while growing up, he added: "It shouldn't define you. I just happen to have CP."

That was also true of Mitte's character Walter 'Flynn' White Jr, the son of Bryan Cranston's character in the drama, which was recently named the best TV show of the 21st Century by the New York Times.

"What I really like is that he was on TV playing a character that had cerebral palsy, but it wasn't about the fact that he had cerebral palsy," says Emma Livingstone, founder and CEO of Up - the Adult Cerebral Palsy Movement.

"When we see RJ Mitte on TV just playing a role, but who also happens to have CP, I think that's really powerful."

Mitte, who died by suicide on Monday at the age of 34, wasn't just an actor - he was also an advocate and supporter, working as an ambassador for charities including United Cerebral Palsy and Can Do Canines, as well as creating The Mitte Foundation, which offered community grants in his home town in Texas.

Susan Sellers, president and CEO of United Cerebral Palsy, says: "His advocacy was rooted in a commitment to ensuring that people with cerebral palsy and other disabilities are seen, heard, and afforded the opportunity to reach their full potential."

Mitte's legacy, particularly for performers with disabilities, is significant.

Ruth Madeley, who stars as disability rights advocate Judy Heumann in new film Being Heumann, tells the BBC: "If you don't see it, you don't think it's possible. When I was younger, acting wasn't even on my radar. I didn't even think it was an option."

The actress, who has spina bifida, adds: "To have people like him [Mitte] on screen for so many young people looking at the arts as an industry that they want to get into... He was just a beautiful example of that.

"But he wasn't just a disabled person breaking down barriers in the industry. He was a phenomenal talent, and I think that's what's going to be missed so much."

Mitte was mobbed by fans on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in 2013

Another actor, Keron Day, who appeared in Netflix hit Sex Education, tells the BBC: "My biggest tribute I can pay to RJ and his work is that I am emailing you today from a set of a TV show.

"That is his legacy: disabled people having careers within the creative industries. If I could have half the impact that RJ has had, I would be enormously proud. It's a sad day for both our industry and our community."

Comedian and screenwriter Laurence Clarke concurs. "The more portrayals that we see on TV, that's going to inspire more disabled people to think it's a career for them," he says.

"Things have moved on a long way since Breaking Bad came out in 2008. But there's always further to go."

Speaking of Mitte's role in Breaking Bad, Clarke tells the BBC: "What's beautiful about it is that the disability is visibly there, always."

He also notes the impact on people watching inclusive dramas and shows.

"The more you're exposed to those portrayals, as members of the public, it becomes just part of life, and how you see the world."

Bryan Cranston (left) played RJ Mitte's dad in the hugely successful Breaking Bad

Mitte was aged three when he was diagnosed with cerebral palsy, which the NHS describes as the name for a group of lifelong conditions that affect movement and co-ordination caused by a problem with the brain that develops around birth.

He was cast in Breaking Bad at 14, and told Channel 4 News in 2016 that the show "pioneered a lot of TV and writers to be more brave".

But he added a note of caution, saying: "We still have a long way to go... it's still a business and we have to do that slowly."

Earlier this month, he hinted that he may be interested in continuing the Breaking Bad story, external, but said any revival would have a lot to live up to.

"I just want to top Breaking Bad, that's the hardest," he said. "I set a bar for myself as a young man that is kinda unattainable. I tell people, 'Look, it's a long way down from the top of the mountain'."

After Breaking Bad, Mitte's other on-screen credits include Hannah Montana, Switched at Birth, Westhampton and his latest project, Talking to Strangers, which came out earlier this year.

But his biggest achievement - and his greatest pride - was his philanthropic work.

"Where I felt most top of the world was being able to help others through Breaking Bad, with the work I've done with people with disabilities... trying to remind people they have a voice and [to] lend my voice.

"The greatest thing that Breaking Bad has given me is to be able to lend my voice to causes that make a meaningful impact, that change people's lives."

#116. Robert Pattinson on new film Primetime and how hunting predators became hit TV

Pattinson says 'Primetime' plot is 'most terrifying' thing that can happen to a parent

Robert Pattinson is having quite the year.

The British actor has already starred opposite Zendaya in The Drama, and played a key role in summer blockbuster The Odyssey.

But his new film, Primetime, takes him in a completely new direction - as he portrays the real-life host of American TV show, To Catch a Predator.

The show, which aired from 2004 to 2007, involved hunting alleged child abusers.

For Pattinson, who became a father almost three years ago, the film's plot is particularly concerning.

"It's both the most terrifying thing that can happen to you, whether you're a parent, or even if you're not," he told BBC News at the film's screening at London Film Festival.

"It's the most unimaginable sin possible," he added.

Robert Pattinson: Being a dad makes life 'more fun'

The new A24 crime thriller depicts the show's host, NBC journalist Chris Hansen, carrying out sting operations on would-be predators.

But it also led to questions over where to draw the line between investigative journalism, police activity and reality television.

Speaking on Sunday night, Pattinson reflected on the show's complicated legacy.

"The show was this kind of microcosm of saying, 'oh, we can do something about [child abuse], and we can do something about it really, really, really quickly," he said.

"And in some ways, that's correct, but it also makes for incredibly powerful TV, and that's when it gets into slightly dicey territory."

Robert Pattinson, who welcomed his first child with Suki Waterhouse in March 2024, says that as a parent, the events depicted in his new film are "terrifying"

When asked whether he thinks attitudes towards entertainment have now changed, Pattinson paused.

"I think on mainstream TV, but then it's just been replaced," he replied, pointing out that similar content has since appeared on social media.

"That's why I was interested in the show, because I could see the beginning of a new wave of 'predator catching' in pretty much the same format that it was in the early 2000s," he said. "And I was just interested as to why that was happening."

"And it got bigger and bigger and bigger, and now it's one of the most massive things on social media."

Lance Oppenheim and Robert Pattinson at London Film Festival's Primetime screening on Sunday night

Hansen himself has been critical of the film, calling it "bizarre" and "detached from reality" in a video posted on X, external.

Addressing his criticisms, director Lance Oppenheim said: "I agree, that was by design.

"I always thought of this movie as more of a fever dream than something that was representational portrait."

Oppenheim added there was something "ancient" about the desire to watch people getting publicly punished.

"It's happened for thousands of years," he added. "I wanted to make something that interrogated that."

Oppenheim, who is also currently co-directing with Nathan Fielder a highly anticipated documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, said separately of that project: "I want everyone to see it. It's a really special movie."

Pattinson, 40, became something of a pin-up after playing vampire Edward Cullen in the Twilight series, alongside American actress Kristen Stewart.

Before that, he stole young hearts as Hufflepuff hunk Cedric Diggory in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire.

He has since starred in major films including Christopher Nolan's Tenet, as well as a range of eccentric, indie films.

This year, he has been on a roll, with Dune: Part Three still to come.

He’s also got the next Batman film in the pipeline, although production on that has reportedly paused, external. When asked when they'll be back to work, Pattinson didn’t give much away ("We don't know yet, but yeah, working on it.")

Primetime has also led to speculation that this could be the year that Pattinson gets his first ever Oscars nomination. Is that likely, I wonder?

"I am eternally grateful that I got these jobs," he responds.

"But then [to have] been able to even do them, this is one of the best years of my life."

#117. Inside the room: What it was like to be with Blackpink's Lisa as race scandal erupted

Lisa, who was born Pranpriya Manobal in Thailand, became one of the world's most-recognisable K-pop idols as a member of Blackpink

What's it like to be the main character of an online scandal?

That's one of the questions raised in a new documentary about Lisa Manobal – one quarter of K-pop phenomenon Blackpink and a breakout star of TV show The White Lotus.

The film captures an unfolding controversy, as leaked videos show Blackpink using racial slurs when they were teenage trainees in the K-pop system.

The clips, which emerged last year, showed the band covering US rap songs during rehearsals. Explicit language, including the n-word, was left uncensored.

The scandal blew up while Lisa was rehearsing for a pivotal performance at the Coachella Festival in 2025.

Offended and upset, some fans demanded an apology - but the band's record label, forbade the members from issuing a statement.

With Lisa's team in crisis mode, documentarian Sue Kim followed Lisa into her dressing room.

"I said, 'Look, I know this is new. I know you guys are wildly confused and hurt, but this is your time to say whatever you want to say - even if you're just processing your thoughts and telling us what you're feeling," Kim tells the BBC.

The film-maker "honestly expected her to say no".

Instead, Lisa lay down on a sofa and spoke from the heart.

"It's bad," the singer says in the documentary, with a mixture of shame and nerves.

Lisa explains she was "15 or 16" when the videos were shot and "didn't know that [word] was sensitive because I'm from Thailand and my first language is not English".

Having only heard the term in rap music, she was unaware of its offensive history.

"Now I would never ever do that because, now, I've got education," she says. "Now I know better.

It is a vulnerable and human response - and nothing like the scripted PR apology you might expect. (Lisa has since apologised publicly, external in an interview with Variety, although some people remained unconvinced, external).

Kim says Lisa’s in-the-moment reaction is "one of the most important scenes" in her documentary, Always Lalisa, which hits cinemas on Monday, 12 October.

"There was no premeditation on Lisa's part, there was no media training," she adds.

"I asked her one question and she just talked for an hour, and everything came out, and it's all stream of consciousness.

"And what you see with Lisa in that moment is so genuine, it's impossible not to feel compassion for her."

Sue Kim (right) followed Lisa for a year, as she launched her solo career during a break in Blackpink's activities

The incident overshadowed what was supposed to be a triumphant launch for Lisa's debut solo album, Alter Ego.

In the film, the singer receives death threats, but presses ahead with public appearances while safety concerns are "spinning in my head".

"To a certain extent I have to take [criticism] and compromise," she says, exhausted, "but sometimes, it's too much".

In a world of sanitised celebrity profiles, Kim's portrayal of upheaval and discomfort is unusual. She asks Lisa about bad reviews, and captures the star being scolded by her vocal coach for lack of effort.

That said, the documentary was commissioned by the film division of the star's record label (which also made the recent, and much less revealing, Oasis documentary), so it is still ultimately a marketing product.

Even the most abrasive moments are calibrated to present Lisa in a good light - but the director credits the star with ensuring the film was not a mere puff piece.

"You never know when you meet an artist how transparent they'll be. And I have to give all credit to Lisa because she allowed us almost total access," Kim says.

"And when I showed her the film, she never asked me to remove a single scene. That's exceptional."

Lisa put aside scandal and online death threats to put on one of the standout performances of 2025's Coachella Music Festival

The documentary captures Lisa's joy - and relief - after she pulled off the hour-long show

The film's main storyline is about Lisa taking a break from K-pop to pursue crossover success in the Western music market.

When we meet her, she is one of the world's most famous women, with millions of record sales and brand deals with Louis Vuitton and Bvlgari.

But she is trapped by a K-pop system that forbids her from drinking alcohol and having adult relationships.

"I don't want my dating to be the thing to hurt Blackpink's popularity," she says in the film. "But when I turned 25, I realised that this is not how you're supposed to live your life."

As a result, Lisa makes an early decision to cut ties with Korean entertainment company YG, who discovered her as a teenager, and signs a new deal with RCA Records in the US.

"Knowing her as I do, that took an immense amount of courage," says Kim.

"In general, she is a very kind, sweet person - and sometimes personalities like that, they don't want to rock the boat.

"Having been trained in the K-pop system from an early age, she grew acclimatised to obedience. Declaring that she wants a break is such a disruption to that way of life that I can only imagine it must have been building inside her for years."

Blackpink are one of K-pop's biggest bands, with hits like Whistle, How You Like That and Kill This Love

The potential rewards for going solo were phenomenal – but so were the risks.

In the film, we see Lisa struggling to assert herself in the recording studio, and tearfully battling nerves over her singing voice.

At the age of 25, she is still curiously child-like. The fierce independence of her solo single New Woman sounds more like aspiration than fact.

Kim says that began to change as they filmed.

"I saw a person who was very tentative and unsure of herself slowly starting to unfold her wings. Making mistakes, but also getting back up on the horse."

Kim locates an inner confidence in early home videos of Lisa competing in talent shows, drawing parallels between that precocious seven-year-old and the young woman who is gradually reclaiming her agency.

She doggedly pursues a role in the third season of hit TV drama The White Lotus, self-taping an audition that wins her the role of kind-hearted wellness coach Mook Sornsin.

On set, she shrugs off the restrictive moral code of her pop career.

"Lisa threw more parties than anyone else," notes the show's executive producer in an interview.

"And the defining characteristic of a Lisa party is tequila shots."

The singer made her acting debut in season three of The White Lotus, filmed on location in her home country

Kim did not partake in the hedonism. In fact, the film-maker and her crew were regularly falling sick as they tried to keep up with Lisa's ridiculous schedule.

"But when we premiered the film in Toronto, Lisa found me and she brought bottles of tequila, and that was like the perfect christening of the film," she laughs.

The movie ends in June 2025 as Lisa returns to Seoul and rejoins Blackpink. As she unpacks her bags, she is clearly conflicted.

"It's bittersweet, and I think that's OK," says Kim.

"I don't think people should take it as like, 'Oh, she hates Blackpink'. It's more that she was reflecting on this year of freedom and worrying that she wouldn't be able to retain that. And that's a very astute fear to have."

Lisa won the award for best pop act at this year's MTV Awards, becoming the first K-pop star to lift the trophy

In the year since, Lisa has already wrapped up her Blackpink duties and started phase two of her solo career with the single Sawadika. Kim says she is not surprised.

"Spending the year away from the K-pop system in the US really opened her horizons," the director says.

"She was exposed to a different kind of entertainment system where they're not held to a vow of chastity. If two star performers link up, it's almost like they get more power.

"That gave her a sense of like, 'Oh, I could have a different life. I might not lose my career if I want to get married and have children'.

"So I think part of the reason why Lisa's interested in continuing her solo career is that it might give her a little bit more personal freedom to be who she is."

#118. Ashe was too scared to cancel her wedding - the story became a hit song

Stop The Wedding is one of the top 10 most-played songs on Spotify this week

No songwriter is ever off duty. And for the US pop singer Ashe, that included her wedding day.

Last October, she was getting ready to tie the knot at a gorgeous hilltop ceremony in Nashville when inspiration struck.

As she watched her family gather, the musician flashed back to her first wedding, almost a decade earlier. The contrast was stark.

She's called that first marriage "horrifying". Her ex, who she met in college, was, she says, emotionally manipulative and psychologically abusive.

He had insisted on a beachfront wedding, which sounds romantic until you learn that Ashe has a fear of the ocean.

In the run-up, she had been tempted to call it off, but felt powerless to stand up for herself.

On her second wedding day, she realised the opposite was true.

"I'm in a happy, healthy relationship and I have total autonomy over my own life," says the singer, now in her early 30s.

"I thought, if this didn't feel right, I could totally put a halt to the whole thing. I definitely didn't have that first time around."

As she adjusted her veil and prepared to walk down the aisle, she filed that feeling away.

Two months later, and back at work, the idea resurfaced and a song spilled out.

It unfolds like a movie scene. Ashe pleads with her younger self to trust her instincts.

"You know how you really feel / You don't have to waste your life," she sings, as the wedding band stutters to an uncertain halt.

"Do I wish I'd had that advice at the time? 1,000 per cent," Ashe says.

"If someone had given me the insight that I was not stuck, and that I could run, I could have changed things sooner. Maybe not at the altar. Maybe weeks before – but it was something I really could have used."

What about the line where she pledges to "burn the wedding dress and run away"?

"I didn't burn my dress," she laughs, "but I did get into a bathtub with it for a photoshoot right after I left my ex-husband, which really ruined it!"

Ashe married her second husband John Clark Canada, drummer for the band The Brook & The Bluff, last year

Released in August, Stop The Wedding this week became one of the 10 most-played songs in the world on Spotify.

On Friday, it broke into the top five of the UK singles chart, while on TikTok, thousands of videos use Ashe's song to highlight red flags in their own relationships.

"I don't think I even let myself dream of this," she says of the song's popularity.

"It's something you hope for when you're first starting out, but when you've been in the business for 10 years, it's a little bit of a shock to the system."

The success is even sweeter because, three years ago, Ashe nearly quit music altogether.

A native of San Jose, she grew up in a conservative household where the radio was permanently tuned to Christian stations.

It was her grandad who introduced her to rock music, playing Tom Petty and Bob Dylan on long road trips. By her teens, she was writing her own music.

After studying orchestral composition at Boston's Berklee College of Music, she moved to Nashville and quickly found work as a songwriter.

She scored an early credit on Demi Lovato's 2017 song You Don't Do It For Me Anymore; but slowly grew frustrated that other people were singing her words.

The decision to become Ashe, whose full name is Ashlyn Rae Willson, didn't happen overnight. She appeared as a featured vocalist on a handful of dance tracks before plunging into a solo career.

"I remember him saying, '[After this] no-one's ever going to love you for you. Anyone you meet now is going to meet you as Ashe, and I met you before'.

"It was truly manipulative, and it kept me stuck. It kept me stuck for a long, long time."

Stop The Wedding is one of the top 10 most-played songs on Spotify this week

It can't be a coincidence that a song she wrote after signing her divorce papers became her breakthrough hit.

Moral of The Story (key lyric: "you can think that you're in love / when you're really just in pain") was released in 2019, and hit one billion streams after appearing in the hit Netflix series To All the Boys: PS I Still Love You.

Ashe was suddenly playing bigger venues and duetting with Niall Horan, but work became all consuming.

When her brother died of an overdose in 2020, she was back on stage within a month.

"There was so much momentum and I was saying yes to far too many things," she reflects now.

"It got to a point where the idea of touring was giving me panic attacks, and I just couldn't stomach being Ashe, which is such a shame, because I'm her."

In 2023, she had a nervous breakdown and stepped away from showbusiness.

"I had to halt everything. I bought a house in Nashville, I gardened, I saw a therapist and I gave myself a chance to miss music."

Finneas O'Connell co-produced Ashe's breakout single Moral of the Story

For six months, she led a quiet, domestic life. But when pop singer Suki Waterhouse invited her to a session, it rekindled her passion for writing.

She made a tentative return with 2024's deeply confessional album Wilson, then teamed up with Billie Eilish's brother Finneas O'Connell to form The Favors, before signing a new deal with Atlantic Records.

Those experiences mean she's treating the success of Stop The Wedding very differently.

"You can get swept up by all the updates on your phone, but this time I'm navigating the emotions of that, and also going for a four-mile walk and calling my mom.

The same can't be said for her new album, The Girl of Your Dreams, which is almost deliriously over the top.

This article contains content provided by Google YouTube. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. You may want to read Google’s cookie policy, external and privacy policy, external before accepting. To view this content choose ‘accept and continue’.

Stop The Wedding sets the tone, with abrupt tempo changes that track Ashe's inner turmoil. Lasso The Moon is more whimsical, setting out the star's outlandish requirements for a new partner.

"God forbid I raise my standards," she laughs.

Love Bomb explores the psychology of a manipulative ex (guess who?); while Swan Lake is a comically villainous portrait of Ashe's possessiveness, complete with a Bugsy Malone chorus line.

It's a deliberately maximalist record, recalling the lush orchestrations of ELO and The Carpenters, with a nod to the revivalist pop of Ashe's friend Laufey.

"We were so bored of making music that's boring," she says.

"It scratches an itch for me as an artist to do something different and not meet the status quo."

The album ends back at her second wedding. The closing track focuses on the "real, true, constant love" she's found with musician John Clark Canada.

"You'll be my Tuesday night and my Sunday drive / And the last speech at my funeral," she sings.

Expanding on that idea, Ashe incorporates the ebullient sound of a New Orleans funeral band in the song's closing moments.

And the person they're burying is the disillusioned girl from Stop The Wedding.

Ashe's album, The Girl of Your Dreams, is out on 16 October.

#119. Screams, haunting scenes and deadly hide-and-seek, as Celebrity Traitors heats up

Friday's episode drew in a peak audience of 9.6 million viewers

Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from the fourth episode of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.

Being a Traitor must be a right nightmare.

While other people are out enjoying their lives, they have to kill it, night after night. Even on the weekend, there is no rest for the wicked.

Friday evening's episode saw the Traitors at it again, murdering Last of Us actor Bella Ramsey, before the faithfuls did their dirty work for them by banishing another of their own, Julie Hesmondhalgh.

The previous night, another faithful, unlucky Industry star Myha'la, had followed self-sabotaging traitor Richard E Grant out of the castle.

And so viewers went into Friday's show knowing that traitors Maya Jama, James Acaster and their newest recruit, Prof Hannah Fry, had been debating murdering one of three Bs: Bella (Ramsey), (James) Blunt and Bash (Sebastian Croft).

When Ramsey failed to arrive for breakfast it soon became apparent what wickedness had taken place overnight.

Emotions run high at the round table as Celebrity Traitors banish two players

Celebrity Traitors cast: Who are this year's 'big dogs' and dark horses

Where is the Traitors castle, and can you visit it?

"That's our biggest threat," explained Jama, in a flashback from the previous night's scenes in the traitors turret. "Get them out the way, that group disperses."

Acaster agreed: "People are doubting their instincts after that roundtable. If Bella's proven to be a faithful, they're going to be even more spun out."

Jama continued: "Chaos, regardless... Bella, you're a genius, but you gotta go."

On receiving the news, Ramsey was shocked but not surprised. "I think this is a clever move by the traitors," they responded in the diary room.

"I was going to re-set and start from the beginning because I got it so wrong with Myha'la.

"So I think that they were right to murder me because I think I would have maybe figured it out."

Bella Ramsey was considered to be the Traitors' "biggest threat" and so had to go

Back at breakfast, Hesmondhalgh's apparently earnest but over-the-top reaction to Ramsey's removal immediately raised suspicions.

The former Coronation Street star had been voted as the most trustworthy of the group by her peers in episode one and given a shield, but that counted for little by episode four.

The cleverest among the group, on paper at least, Fry, found questions being asked of her again too as the day rolled on.

"I did not choose the traitor life, the traitor life chose me," said the latest recruit to the dark side. "I know there are people who are suspicious of me but I'm going to enjoy every last moment."

Comedian and Miss Marple impersonator Miranda Hart is one of them. "Hannah lied to us," she rightly noted, with reference to the professor's confusing shield story that helped to see off Myha'la the night before.

Singer and ex-military man James Blunt, however, had other ideas, ramping up his campaign against Hesmondhalgh, whom he believed to be a little too trustworthy to be true.

The group conversing with the grateful dead inside the haunted cabin

Romesh Ranganathan lets out a scream while salvaging a dead woman's wedding dress

Friday's mission raised more money for charity and also raised spirits, but not in a good way.

It involved the group paying a visit to a graveside haunted cabin to converse with the dead about unresolved matters.

"It's creepy, it's giving murder," noted Barbie actress Sharon Rooney on arrival.

Comedian Romesh Ranganathan joked that his mum was going to "absolutely hate this", as the group gathered in a graveside chant led by the booming voice of big dog actor Michael Sheen.

The spooky task made Ranganathan himself let out a hellish scream and saw Hart come face-to face with a masked hooded creature, before team-player Croft volunteered to go head-first into a stinky old toilet in scenes resembling ITV's I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here.

"Guys, it's a little bit of poo," noted hardman Ross Kemp, as all around him gagged. "It's not gonna kill you."

Actor Croft received a protective shield for his troubles, at least. "If I'd have put my hands and head down a toilet for nothing, I would've been fuming," he fairly noted.

Watch on iPlayer with new episodes every Thursday and Friday

The latest banished and murdered celebs have their say in Uncloaked

The group, with a little help from the undead, had to find a child's toys and a woman's wedding dress and shoes. This later prompted model Jerry Hall to reminisce about her own wedding to Rolling Stones frontman Mick Jagger.

"Before I got married to Mick - we'd already been together seven years, had two children - I put on a wedding dress every day until he agreed that we get married," she revealed.

Some rancid wine that tasted like "salty bin juice", according to comedian Joanne McNally, topped off possibly the most revolting task yet.

On the way back to the castle, YouTuber King Kenny raised more suspicions about Fry having allowed him to grab a shield. "She held off to make herself look a bit innocent," he told his fellow faithfuls.

Traitor Jama smartly deflected attention away from herself by latching on to the growing suspicions around Hesmondhalgh.

James Blunt led the charge against faithful Julie Hesmondhalgh and has seemingly now put himself in the frame as a result

Ahead of the roundtable, Fry told producers she knew she would have to fight like her life depended on it - because it did - and try to disguise herself as still being a faithful.

Once discussions were under way, she played the sympathy card, claiming she had been left feeling "vulnerable" as she knew her reputation as a brain box would make her a target.

Miss Marple aka Hart wasn't going to let her off the hook that easily, however, noting how Fry's argument the previous night had contradicted that of the innocent but now sadly now departed Myha'la.

In a nice moment of levity in another tense debate, comedian Joe Lycett reminded the traitors - and pointedly, Hesmondhalgh - that he would "like to be recruited at some stage". He stressed: "I'm still very much available."

Hesmondhalgh laughed about how "going all dry mouthed" while defending herself was not helping her cause.

"It would be a cruel move, wouldn't it?" noted Sheen. "To take the most trusted of our group and make them the most suspected."

Ranganathan offered: "The person that we nominated as our most trustworthy person, we have now completely flipped on."

Hesmondhalgh bade farewell to her fellow faithfuls, describing the show's reveal as "iconic"

The conclusion was to banish Hesmondhalgh, who, in her parting words, said it had been an "immense experience".

"Alas," she continued, confirming her fidelity as tears appeared in eyes around the table: "It may mean I am not a phenomenal actor."

Singer Blunt, who had led the charge against her, appears to have now put himself in the frame. He told the group: "I'm so sorry, that's my fault."

"He's been wrong about every theory he's came up with," said Rooney, privately.

"So have I!" replied a frustrated McNally.

Hart declared that "everything is up in the air" now, following Hesmondhalgh's eviction, which King Kenny called the team's "biggest loss" so far.

First recruit, Acaster's strategy is to simply continue playing the game as if he is a faithful, he said. Jama is clearly loving life on the dark side and leaning into it, while Fry, it's fair to say, is finding it tougher.

"You two saved me," Fry told the other two of her stressful day, while back in the turret in their cloaks.

Jama, who is now firmly the ringleader of the tormentors, demanded that her conscripted co-conspirators now "snap into murder mode".

The episode ended not with a murder but a fresh twist - the promise of a deathly game of hide-and-seek for four chosen contestants.

Ross Kemp, Rob Beckett, Leigh-Anne Pinnock and Romesh Ranganathan looking delighted to have been chosen for a game of killer hide-and-seek

The traitors opted to stay out of the game themselves, before settling on Kemp, Ranganathan, his comic pal Rob Beckett and Little Mix and solo singer Leigh-Anne Pinnock.

"I think this is gonna mess with everybody's heads," said Fry.

Presenter Claudia Winkleman greeted the four of them outside the castle in the dead of night.

"If only it was that easy Romesh," replied the host, explaining how when they go down to the woods tonight they'll be sure of a big surprise: one of them will be killed face-to-face.

Only Pinnock, it was decided democratically, will be immune from murder in the castle crypt game within a game thanks to a special key, though the Traitors aren't to know it.

All this mischief and terror and it's not Halloween for weeks yet.

Newfound Traitor Hannah Fry survived a stressful episode

The public appetite for treachery is strong, it seems.

Friday's episode drew in a peak audience of 9.6 million viewers, just short of the 10.3 million people who tuned in for Thursday's offering.

It comes after the opening episode of the Celebrity Traitors' second season became the most-watched debut of any series of the programme in the UK to date, attracting 8.9 million viewers.

Celebrity Traitors continues on Thursday at 20:00 BST on BBC One and iPlayer.

Have you played a version of the Traitors or another social deduction game at home or socially? Share your experience.

#120. Olivia Colman on viral Wicker memes: 'This has never happened to me before'

Olivia Colman stars alongside Alexander Skarsgård in new film Wicker

It has already been described as 2026's weirdest rom-com, external.

And new film Wicker has sparked a deluge of viral memes and steamy jokes that have flooded social media ahead of its release.

Speaking to the BBC at its London Film Festival premiere, lead star Olivia Colman said she never expected such a big reaction.

"No, literally this has never happened for anything I've done before," she said.

"But you put Alexander Skarsgård in an interesting outfit, and everyone is looking."

The film tells the tale of a lonely, ostracised fisherwoman (Colman) living in a medieval village.

Tired of constantly being mocked for being single, she hires a basketmaker to mould her a new partner made entirely out of wicker.

Enter Skarsgård - but not as you've ever seen him before.

As the "wicker husband", he emerges as a strapping, dashing life-size piece of furniture.

And he proves to be a devoted partner, and passionate lover, sparking jealousy among the other village women.

Wicker has an A-list cast, with other stars including Peter Dinklage as the basket weaver, Elizabeth Debicki as the tailor's wife, and Richard E Grant as the village doctor.

The film has had mixed reviews from critics, with the Telegraph giving it just one star, external and calling it "a mortifying adult fairy tale", but the Times awarded four stars, external, mainly for Colman's "astonishing performance".

But since the release of the trailer, there's been a huge buzz from audiences online - from BookTok and FilmTok fans swooning over Skarsgård’s character, to questions being asked over splinter risks during the film's erotic scenes.

Swedish giant Ikea even got involved, posting photos of its rattan furniture on Instagram in a nod to the film, with the caption “husband material”.

When asked why she thinks people are so fascinated and so thirsty for the wicker husband, Colman answered: "We all love a little bit of escapism. That's what film is beautiful for.

"And it's magical, and a bit of fantasy, and people love that, especially currently. What's not to love about a little bit of escapism and fantasy?"

She also said it was the film's originality that drew her to it.

Left-right: Elizabeth Debicki, Alexander Skarsgård and Olivia Colman

Skarsgård's see-through shoes attracted attention on the red carpet

"You get a lot of scripts through the post, and you feel like you've seen a bit before. And this, I really hadn't seen this before, so I was excited," she said.

Like Colman, Debicki agrees that Skarsgård is the main reason the film has lit up the internet.

"I think it was a lot to do with Alex in a wicker man costume, really," she told the BBC. "I think that's something that apparently everybody would like to see."

But Skarsgård himself gives all the credit to the designers of the outfit. "All I had to do was get stuck into it," he says.

He also said the sex scenes were "super fun" to shoot.

"We wanted those moments when the bed crashes and breaks, and the way they comment on that in the scene is quite comedic," he said.

"But [the characters] also have tender moments and sexy moments, it was great."

The steamy new rom-com has been causing a stir at film festivals

The film is based on the short story The Wicker Husband by Ursula Wills-Jones.

After its premiere at Sundance film festival earlier this year, The Guardian awarded it, external two stars, praising the "eye-catching premise" but cautioning that there was "too much wood but not enough fire".

But The Hollywood Reporter, external was more positive, calling it "a warming, sometimes poignant pleasure".

Away from the social media buzz, the film's stars say it also taps into deeper themes, from gender roles to breaking societal rules.

"It's very funny and strange and wonderful, but I find it very moving. And it's a good one to discover beyond the Ikea memes," said Debicki.

"It touches on a lot of stuff. Hierarchy, social structure," said Skarsgård. "But it's done with such a light touch."

"It's about love, and it is funny, but it's also a romance, and it very gently laughs at the sort of traditions we have in marriage and community," said Colman.

"I think it's something that you will come out and discuss a lot."

Wicker is released in UK cinemas on October 30.
